# Global knitr options
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,

# Load libraries - loading dplyr AFTER plyr to prevent function masking

# Buck's packages have to be installed in this order
# devtools::install_github("wStockhausen/wtsQMD")
# devtools::install_github("wStockhausen/wtsUtilities")
# devtools::install_github("wStockhausen/wtsPlots")
# devtools::install_github("wStockhausen/tcsamFunctions")
# devtools::install_github("wStockhausen/rTCSAM02")
# devtools::install_github("wStockhausen/wtsMarkdown")
# devtools::install_github("wStockhausen/rCompTCMs")
# devtools::install_github("wStockhausen/wtsGMACS")

# Mapping and Analysis
pacman::p_load(PBSmodelling, PBSmapping, maps, mapproj, ggridges)

# Additional utilities
pacman::p_load(coda, plotrix, miceadds)

# Pander options for cleaner tables
panderOptions('table.alignment.default', 'left')
panderOptions('table.split.table', Inf)


#  --- Load model results ----
# Ensure rda_ModelsResLst.RData is in the working directory
# it contains all the results from '05_buck_read_results.R"
reslst <- wtsUtilities::getObj("Models/rda_ModelsResLst.RData")

# Extract case names
cases <- names(reslst$repsLst)
nCases <- length(cases)

# Create a clean string for referencing models in the text
# Converts "25_1_gmacs" to "25.1.gmacs"
clean_cases <- gsub("_", ".", cases)
strMdls <- ifelse(nCases == 1, "model", "models")

# Build the descriptive string (e.g., "model A, model B, and model C")
if (nCases > 1) {
  strCases <- paste(paste(clean_cases[-nCases], collapse = ", "), 
                    "and", clean_cases[nCases])
} else {
  strCases <- clean_cases
}

# --- Report Configuration ---
ABC_buffer     <- 0.8
chosen_ind     <- 1
OFL_fleet_ind  <- 0
source("0-models.R") # Load model definitions

# model_defs is now the September set exactly (pruned 2026-08-28), so this is
# normally all of it. It stays as a guard: a model that has not been built yet
# drops out of the tables and the narrative count instead of rendering as a row
# of NAs or zeros. 0-models.R warns by name when that happens. Narrative model
# counts must use n_models, never length(model_defs).
models_present <- model_defs[dir.exists(model_defs)]
n_models       <- length(models_present)

## --- Tier 4: the 2026 harvest specification -------------------------------
## SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for the specification scalars. Every downstream
## section (Exec Summary items 5-7, the OFL and ABC sections, status determination,
## Appendix B) must read THESE names and never recompute them -- that is how two
## tables in one document end up disagreeing.
##
## Source is the CSV 07_calc_tier4.R writes. The Phase-1 sketch (§15a) guessed
## at "Models/tier4_results.rds" with a [[VERIFY]] on it; 07 writes a CSV, not an
## RDS, and there is no tier4$by_currency list. Interface is
## currency/Bmsy/B_curr/status/M/Fofl/OFL plus the alternatives.
##
## BASIS (backlog 7d/7e): flat F_OFL = M above the beta closure, following the
## groundfish Tier 5 FMP, with OFL = F_OFL * B to match other BSAI crab Tier 4
## assessments. The ramped-HCR and Baranov alternatives are carried alongside
## for reporting; neither is the basis.
TIER4_CSV <- "data/tier4/tier4_by_currency.csv"
if (file.exists(TIER4_CSV)) {
  tier4_by_currency <- read.csv(TIER4_CSV, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  t4_rec <- tier4_by_currency[tier4_by_currency$currency == "morphometric", ]
  stopifnot("tier4_by_currency.csv has no single morphometric row" = nrow(t4_rec) == 1)
  bmsy_2026        <- t4_rec$Bmsy      # mean REMA-smoothed biomass, years < BMSY_WINDOW_END
  mmb_2026         <- t4_rec$B_curr    # terminal-year REMA-smoothed morphometric MMB
  status_2026      <- t4_rec$status    # mmb_2026 / bmsy_2026
  fofl_2026        <- t4_rec$Fofl
  ofl_2026         <- t4_rec$OFL
  ## Uncertainty on the biomass the control rule uses. Required for Tiers 4-5
  ## by the groundfish guidelines (4.11.2); derivation stated in Section F.
  ## REMA's 95% prediction interval on the SMOOTHED series -- NOT the survey's
  ## own sampling CV, which is an input to that fit.
  mmb_2026_lci     <- t4_rec$B_curr_lci
  mmb_2026_uci     <- t4_rec$B_curr_uci
  mmb_2026_cv      <- t4_rec$B_curr_cv
  ## Propagated to status and OFL. F_OFL is flat at M throughout the interval
  ## (status stays above the closure threshold at both ends), so the OFL
  ## interval is just the biomass interval scaled by F.
  status_2026_lci  <- mmb_2026_lci / bmsy_2026
  status_2026_uci  <- mmb_2026_uci / bmsy_2026
  ofl_2026_lci     <- fofl_2026 * mmb_2026_lci
  ofl_2026_uci     <- fofl_2026 * mmb_2026_uci
  ofl_2026_ramp    <- t4_rec$OFL_ramp     # sensitivity: ramped HCR
  ofl_2026_baranov <- t4_rec$OFL_baranov  # alternative equation, author recommendation
  NAT_M            <- t4_rec$M            # target F; read, not restated

  ## BMSY_WINDOW_END is a constant inside 07_calc_tier4.R and is not carried in
  ## its output, so the document cannot simply read it. Rather than restate the
  ## literal and let the two drift, recover it: B_MSY is the mean of the REMA
  ## series over years strictly before the cutoff, so the correct cutoff is the
  ## one that reproduces the stored B_MSY. If none does, the constant in 07 has
  ## changed and the document says so instead of printing a stale year.
  BMSY_WINDOW_END <- NA_integer_
  if (file.exists("data/tier4/rema_predictions.csv")) {
    .rp <- read.csv("data/tier4/rema_predictions.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    .rp <- .rp[.rp$size == "morphometric", ]
    if (nrow(.rp)) {
      .cand <- sort(unique(.rp$Year))
      .fit  <- vapply(.cand, function(y) {
        v <- .rp$rema_pred[.rp$Year < y]
        if (!length(v)) NA_real_ else abs(mean(v) - bmsy_2026)
      }, numeric(1))
      if (any(is.finite(.fit)) && min(.fit, na.rm = TRUE) < 1e-6)
        BMSY_WINDOW_END <- .cand[which.min(.fit)]
    }
  }
} else {
  ## Stub so the document still knits before 07 has been run. The empty frame
  ## matters: the Tier 4 and ABC sections select rows out of tier4_by_currency
  ## by currency, and without it those lookups error the knit rather than
  ## printing the not-yet-computed marker.
  tier4_by_currency <- data.frame(
    currency = character(0), Bmsy = numeric(0), B_curr = numeric(0),
    status = numeric(0), Fofl = numeric(0), OFL = numeric(0),
    Fofl_ramp = numeric(0), OFL_ramp = numeric(0), OFL_baranov = numeric(0),
    M = numeric(0), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  bmsy_2026 <- mmb_2026 <- status_2026 <- fofl_2026 <- ofl_2026 <- NA_real_
  ofl_2026_ramp <- ofl_2026_baranov <- NA_real_
  mmb_2026_lci <- mmb_2026_uci <- mmb_2026_cv <- NA_real_
  status_2026_lci <- status_2026_uci <- ofl_2026_lci <- ofl_2026_uci <- NA_real_
  NAT_M <- NA_real_
  BMSY_WINDOW_END <- NA_integer_
}
## Inline text uses these; render them as a visible marker rather than "NA".
## Length-0 is treated like NA: a currency lookup that matches no row must print
## the marker, not abort the knit on `if (logical(0))`.
.f  <- function(v, d = 3) if (length(v) != 1L || is.na(v)) "[[not yet computed]]" else sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), v)
.fy <- function(v) if (is.na(v)) "[[unrecovered -- BMSY_WINDOW_END changed in 07]]" else as.character(v)
msst_2026 <- 0.5 * bmsy_2026
abc_2026  <- ABC_buffer * ofl_2026    # ABC_buffer <- 0.8, set above

## --- Observed survey biomass, all three currencies -------------------------
## OBSERVED survey estimates, distinct from the REMA-smoothed B_curr the Tier 4
## calculation uses. Read from data, never hardcoded, so the text cannot drift
## from the survey pull. All in kt.
##   morphometric mature male -> data/derived/survey_indices.csv (the model input)
##   >=95 mm  ("large_male")     -> 02's crabpack pull, BIOMASS_MT
##   >101 mm  ("preferred_male") -> same file
## 2026 is the terminal survey; 2025 is the preceding one, which is what the
## October specification is compared against.
.svy_num <- function(x) if (length(x) == 1L) as.numeric(x) else NA_real_
if (file.exists("data/derived/survey_indices.csv")) {
  .si <- read.csv("data/derived/survey_indices.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  .mm <- .si[.si$sex == "male" & .si$maturity == "mature", ]
  survey_morph_2025 <- .svy_num(.mm$biomass[.mm$year == 2025])
  survey_morph_2026 <- .svy_num(.mm$biomass[.mm$year == 2026])
} else survey_morph_2025 <- survey_morph_2026 <- NA_real_

if (file.exists("data/survey/survey_large_male_index_derived.csv")) {
  .lg <- read.csv("data/survey/survey_large_male_index_derived.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  .get <- function(cat, yr) .svy_num(.lg$BIOMASS_MT[.lg$CATEGORY == cat & .lg$YEAR == yr]) / 1000
  survey_large_2025 <- .get("large_male", 2025);     survey_large_2026 <- .get("large_male", 2026)
  survey_pref_2025  <- .get("preferred_male", 2025); survey_pref_2026  <- .get("preferred_male", 2026)
} else survey_large_2025 <- survey_large_2026 <- survey_pref_2025 <- survey_pref_2026 <- NA_real_

## Tier 4 results for ALL THREE currencies, for the comparison table in Section F.
if (exists("tier4_by_currency")) {
  tier4_all <- tier4_by_currency[, intersect(
    c("currency","Bmsy","B_curr","status","M","Fofl","OFL","OFL_ramp","OFL_baranov"),
    names(tier4_by_currency))]
} else tier4_all <- NULL

# Case selection
# SEPTEMBER 2026 PORT — repointed from the May candidate bracket to the accepted model.
# Accepted (RECOMMENDED) model = "26.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + new_mat)"
# (Models/26_gmacs_update_newmat_plus_group, shortname Model 25.2e (new data)) -- May's 25.2c advanced to
# end year 2025, i.e. fishery through 2025 and survey through 2026. Repointed 2026-08-28; it
# previously named the *May* folder (terminal 2024), which would have reported the wrong fit.
# Reference (2025 accepted, rolled forward) = "25.1 gmacs" (Models/25_gmacs).
# These names must match the case names produced when rda_ModelsResLst.RData is regenerated (03_build_results_object.R).
# >>> REVIEW: confirm comparison pairs once the 2026 results object exists.
accepted_model      <- "26.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + new_mat)"
reference_model     <- "25.1 gmacs"
case_for_resids     <- accepted_model                            # model to print size-comp residuals for
case_for_data_table <- c(reference_model, accepted_model)
case_for_mat_plot   <- c(reference_model, accepted_model)        # show effect of new maturity (reference lacks new_mat)
report_model <- model_defs[accepted_model]


# Global Switches
do_size_comps  <- 1 # Set to 1 to regenerate PNGs (can take time)
do_proj        <- 0 # Set to 1 to process projection files
make_proj_fig  <- 0 # Set to 1 to generate projection plots

# --- Plot size comp ----
if(do_size_comps==1){
  # Extract results using Buck's package tools
  dfrZCs <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Size_fit_summary") |> 
    dplyr::mutate(across(c(year, size, inpSS, inpN, aggObs, aggPrd, aggRes), as.numeric))
  
  # 2. Assign models to Groups
  # Maturity ogive and hybrid status will affect
  dfrZCs <- dfrZCs |> 
    dplyr::mutate(
      fleet = dplyr::case_when(
        grepl("compfix", case, ignore.case = TRUE) & fleet == "Pot_Fishery" ~ "Pot_fishery_compfix",
        grepl("hyb_surv|hyb_both", case, ignore.case = TRUE) & fleet == "NMFS_Trawl_1982" ~ "NMFS_Trawl_1982_hybrid",
        grepl("hyb_surv|hyb_both", case, ignore.case = TRUE) & fleet == "NMFS_Trawl_1989" ~ "NMFS_Trawl_1989_hybrid",
        .default = fleet
      ),
      fleet = ifelse(
        grepl("plus group", case, ignore.case = TRUE) & fleet == "Pot_Fishery", "Pot_fishery_plus_group", fleet),
      fleet = ifelse(
        grepl("hyb_fishery|hyb_both", case, ignore.case = TRUE) & fleet == "Pot_Fishery", "Pot_fishery_hybrid", fleet),
    maturity_ogive = ifelse(grepl("new_mat", case, ignore.case = TRUE), 
                           "New maturity", 
                           "Old maturity"),
    ) |>
    dplyr::group_by(fleet, maturity_ogive, comp_type, sex, maturity) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(comp_id = dplyr::cur_group_id())
  
  # Plotting Logic
  unique_comps <- dfrZCs |> distinct(comp_id, aggID, fleet, comp_type, sex, maturity_ogive, maturity, shell_cond, case) # Grant: case, may not be needed...
  
  for (i in seq_along(unique(unique_comps$comp_id))) { # Loop around comp data types
    curr_id <- i
    tmp     <- dfrZCs |> filter(comp_id == curr_id)
    
    # Size Composition Plot (use shortnames in the legend)
    tmp$case_short <- to_short(tmp$case)
    p <- ggplot(tmp) +
      geom_bar(aes(x = as.numeric(size), y = aggObs), stat = "identity", position = "identity", fill = 'lightgrey') +
      geom_line(aes(x = as.numeric(size), y = aggPrd, col = case_short)) +
      facet_wrap(~year) +
      theme_bw() +
      labs(x = "Carapace width (mm)", y = "Proportion", col = "Model",
           title = paste(tmp$fleet[1], tmp$sex[1], tmp$comp_type[1], tmp$maturity[1], tmp$maturity_ogive[1],  sep = " / "))
    
    compname <- paste(tmp$fleet[1], tmp$sex[1], tmp$comp_type[1], tmp$maturity[1], tmp$maturity_ogive[1], sep = "_")
    ggsave(paste0("plots/size_comp_plot_",  curr_id, "_", compname, ".png"), p, height = 8, width = 8, dpi = 300)
    
    # Residual Plot for specific case
    res_data <- tmp |> 
      filter(case == case_for_resids) |> 
      mutate(raw_res = aggObs - aggPrd)
    
    p_res <- ggplot(res_data) +
      geom_point(aes(x = year, y = size, size = abs(raw_res), col = as.factor(sign(raw_res))), alpha = 0.9) +
      theme_bw() +
      labs(x = "Year", y = "Carapace width (mm)", col = "Residual direction", size = "Raw residual size")
    
    ggsave(paste0("plots/size_comp_resid_", curr_id, "_", compname, ".png"), p_res, height = 10, width = 8, dpi = 300)
  }
}




#=================================
# this code pulls the projections for selected models
# to do the projections, follow these steps:
# this requires a converged model with a hessian
# make a new folder with the model to project in it, specify projection details in .PROJ file
# .PROJ file needs to change strategies
# save .par file as .pin file
# run '.\gmacs.exe -phase 6 -nohess -mcmc 1 -mcsave 1'
# that executes one draw (at the MLE) of MCMC and saves the results
# run '.\gmacs.exe -mceval -noest' in that folder to write output to 'mcoutPROJ.REP'
# run code below to pull relevant info, be sure to modify years to make 'mcoutPROJ.REP'

# BE SURE TO CHANGE THE F IN THE PROJ FILE TO THE FOFL
proj_dir <- file.path(getwd(), report_model)

if(do_proj==1)
{
  proj_dirs<-c(paste(proj_dir,"proj/mcoutPROJSSB.REP",sep=''))
  
  proj_mmb_under_ofl<-rep(NA,length(proj_dirs))
  proj_stat_ofl<-rep(NA,length(proj_dirs))
  proj_mmb_under_nof<-rep(NA,length(proj_dirs))
  proj_stat_nof<-rep(NA,length(proj_dirs))
  
  for(x in 1:length(proj_dirs))
  {
    innames<-c("Draw","Replicate","Treatment",paste("F",seq(1,4)),
               "B35",seq(1982,2035))
    projfile<-as.data.frame(matrix(scan(proj_dirs[x],skip=1),ncol=length(innames),byrow=TRUE))
    colnames(projfile)<-innames
    
    proj_mmb_under_ofl[x]<-filter(projfile,Treatment==2)$'2025'[1]
    proj_stat_ofl[x]<-proj_mmb_under_ofl[x]/filter(projfile,Treatment==2)$'B35'[1]
    
    proj_mmb_under_nof[x]<-filter(projfile,Treatment==1)$'2025'[1]
    proj_stat_nof[x]<- proj_mmb_under_nof[x]/filter(projfile,Treatment==2)$'B35'[1]
  }
}


if(make_proj_fig==1)
{
  #==make a figure that shows projections under given assumptions about rec and M and F
  yams<-melt(projfile[,c(1,2,3,4,9:ncol(projfile))],id.vars=c("Draw","Replicate","Treatment","F 1"))
  yams$Treatment<-c("No fishing","OFL")[yams$Treatment]
  meds<-yams%>%
    group_by(Treatment,variable)%>%
    summarize(med_ssb=median(value))
  
  #==compare to survey biomass
  tmp<-readLines(paste(report_model,"/Gmacsall.out",sep=''))   # was model_defs[1] (reference); use the accepted report model, which is guaranteed run
  male_wt_len<-as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[names(report_model)]]$IndivWeightByXM,Sex=="male"&Year=="1982"&Maturity=='mature')[,4:25])
  
  #==mature males
  st<-grep(c("N(males): dataframe"),tmp,fixed=TRUE)
  tmp2<-tmp[st:(st+50)]
  tmp3<-tmp2[grep("1982",tmp2)[1]:(grep("EOD",tmp2)-1)]
  
  N_males<-NULL
  for(x in 1:length(tmp3))
    N_males<-rbind(N_males,as.numeric(unlist(strsplit(tmp3[x],split=" "))))
  
  
  sweep1<-sweep(N_males[,3:ncol(N_males)],2,male_wt_len,FUN='*')
  sizes<-seq(27.5,132.5,5)
  mat_95<-rep(0,length(sizes))
  mat_95[sizes>95]<-1  
  mat_95[sizes<95&sizes>90]<-0.5
  sweep2<-apply(sweep(sweep1,2,mat_95,FUN='*'),1,sum)/1000000
  surv_lg_male<-data.frame(Year=N_males[,1],MMB=sweep2)
  
  png(paste("plots/projections.png",sep=""),height=8,width=8,res=300,units='in')
  ggplot()+
    geom_line(data=yams,aes(x=as.numeric(as.character(variable)),y=value,col=as.factor(Treatment),group=interaction(Replicate,Treatment)),alpha=.3)+
    geom_line(data=meds,aes(x=as.numeric(as.character(variable)),y=med_ssb,col=as.factor(Treatment)),lwd=2)+
    geom_line(data=filter(meds,as.numeric(as.character(variable))<2026),aes(x=as.numeric(as.character(variable)),y=med_ssb,col=as.factor(Treatment)),lwd=2,col='grey')+
    theme_bw()+ylab("MMB (>=95mm)")+
    xlab("Year")+labs(color="Fishing")+ylim(0,900)+
    geom_line(data=surv_lg_male,aes(x=Year,y=MMB))
  dev.off()
}

# Executive Summary

This document is the September 2026 stock assessment for eastern Bering Sea (EBS) snow crab (*Chionoecetes opilio*), prepared for the Crab Plan Team and the Scientific and Statistical Committee, and provides the basis for the 2026/27 harvest specifications.

The stock was declared overfished in October 2021 and is rebuilding under Amendment 53. The directed fishery was closed for the 2022 and 2023 seasons and has since reopened at a reduced scale, with 4.13 kt retained in 2025/26. Mature male biomass is estimated at `r .f(mmb_2026, 1)` kt, or `r .f(100*status_2026, 0)` percent of the B~MSY~ proxy of `r .f(bmsy_2026, 1)` kt, and is above the minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 1)` kt. The stock is therefore not overfished on the current estimate, and the point estimate has not reached the biomass at which it would be considered rebuilt. The 95 percent interval on that biomass runs from `r .f(mmb_2026_lci, 1)` to `r .f(mmb_2026_uci, 1)` kt: the stock is above the minimum stock size threshold across the whole of it, but its upper end reaches the B~MSY~ proxy, so the rebuilt threshold is not excluded.

Following the June 2026 SSC recommendation, the overfishing limit is calculated under Tier 4 while a simpler and more stable Tier 3 model is developed. The recommended OFL is `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt, and the ABC after a `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` percent buffer is `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt. [[author: confirm the buffer, and state the currency and control rule the recommendation rests on -- the choice of currency changes the OFL by more than a factor of four (Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies)), and the September 2025 assessment recommended >= 95 mm carapace width rather than morphometric maturity.]]

`r n_models` models are presented. Model 25.2e (new data) is the author-recommended Tier 3 model and carries the corrections endorsed by the CPT in May 2026 and the SSC in June 2026; two sensitivities examine the removal of the female population and the truncation of the data to 2019. The Tier 3 models are presented to document progress and are not proposed for specification. Convergence remains the principal difficulty: jittering continues to locate multiple optima whose separation in likelihood is small but whose management quantities differ materially.

[[author: the SAFE guidelines specify ten numbered Executive Summary items -- stock, catches, data sources, stock biomass, recruitment, a management performance table, a basis-for-the-OFL table, the OFL probability distribution, the ABC basis, and a rebuilding summary. Items 6 and 7 are tables that have not yet been built.]]

\newpage

# A. Summary of Major Changes

1. **Management:** The eastern Bering Sea snow crab population was declared overfished in October 2021 and the directed fishery was closed by the State of Alaska for the 2022 and 2023 seasons. A small fishery occurred in 2024, with 2.15 kt retained, and a larger one in 2025, with 4.13 kt retained. The stock remains under a rebuilding plan.

2. **Input data:** The 2026 NMFS summer trawl survey and the 2025 fishery data have been added. Three corrections have been made to the inputs themselves. The total-male size composition has been corrected, resolving a discrepancy between the file used in September 2025 and the file produced by the script that translates the ADF&G delivery. The plus group has been enlarged to include all crab greater than 135 mm carapace width, which the previous configuration discarded. The size-composition bin convention has been changed so that a crab falling exactly on a 5 mm cutoff is assigned to the upper bin, and a transcription error in the growth data has been corrected, a 26.3 mm crab's molt increment having been recorded as 73 mm rather than 7.3 mm. Hybrid *Chionoecetes* catch and survey data were evaluated in the May 2026 preliminary assessment and are not included in any model presented here, following CPT and SSC advice; an immature survey index was likewise evaluated and is not carried forward.

3. **Assessment methodology:** Management quantities were derived from maximum likelihood estimates of model parameters in a size-based, integrated assessment method using GMACS, version 2.20.34. Retrospective and jittering analyses were performed for four of the six models presented (Table \@ref(tab:model-overview)); Model 25 and Model 25.2e were not re-run for either. The probability of terminal molt at size is now taken from the maturity workflow developed by the Kodiak laboratory (Ryznar, in prep) rather than the design-based series used previously. Fits that did not meet the conventional maximum-gradient criterion were polished with Newton steps taken using the inverse Hessian, which reduces the gradient without materially moving the fit. Following the June 2026 SSC recommendation, the Tier 4 calculation is brought forward as the basis for the harvest specification while a simpler and more stable Tier 3 model is developed; the Tier 3 models are presented to document progress and are not proposed for specification.

4. **Assessment results:** [[author: state the recommended OFL and ABC for 2026, the tier and currency they rest on, and the F~OFL~ applied, in the same form as the 2025 document. Two comparisons against 2025 are available and they tell different stories, so state which one is meant. The 2025 *author-preferred* OFL was 3.26 kt at F~OFL~ = 0.18, on Tier 3 with >= 95 mm carapace width as the currency; the specification the SSC went on to adopt for 2025/26 was Tier 4b with an OFL of 20.11 kt and an ABC of 12.07 kt. The 2025 *Tier 4* calculation, which is the like-for-like comparison now that the SSC has directed Tier 4 for this cycle, gave 28.41, 8.64 and 6.11 kt on the morphometric, >= 95 mm and > 101 mm currencies against 30.765, 6.620 and 4.591 kt this cycle -- higher on morphometric by 8% and lower on both large-male currencies by about 24%.]]

# C. Introduction

Studies and data relevant to key population and fishery processes are discussed below to provide background for the modeling choices made in this assessment. A model description is available on the github repository for GMACS and the files needed to reproduce these assessments also have a github repo, both of which are linked at the end of this document.

## Distribution
Snow crab (*Chionoecetes opilio*) are distributed on the continental shelf of the Bering Sea, Chukchi Sea, and in the western Atlantic Ocean as far south as Maine.  In the Bering Sea, snow crab are distributed widely over the shelf and are common at depths less than ~200 meters (see tech memo; Zacher et al., 2025). Smaller crab tend to occupy more inshore northern regions and mature crab occupy deeper areas to the south of the juveniles (see Zacher et al., 2025; Zheng et al. 2001). The eastern Bering Sea population within U.S. waters is managed as a single stock; however, the distribution of the population may extend into Russian waters to an unknown degree.

## Natural Mortality

Relatively few targeted studies exist to determine natural mortality for snow crab in the Bering Sea.  Nevissi, et al. (1995) used radiometric techniques to estimate shell age from last molt (\autoref{nevissi}).  The total sample size was 21 male crab (a combination of Tanner and snow crab) from a collection of 105 male crab from various hauls in the 1992 National Marine Fishery Service (NMFS) Bering Sea survey. Representative samples for the 5 shell condition categories were collected from the available crab.  Shell condition 5 crab (SC5 = very, very old shell) had a maximum age of 6.85 years (s.d. 0.58, 95% CI approximately 5.69 to 8.01 years; carapace width of 110 mm).  The average age of 6 crab with SC4 (very old shell) and SC5, was 4.95 years (range: 2.70 to 6.85 years).  Given the small sample size, this maximum age may not represent the 1.5% percentile of the population that is approximately equivalent to Hoenig's method (1983). Tag recovery evidence from eastern Canada revealed observed maximum ages in exploited populations of 17-19 years (Nevissi, et al. 1995, Sainte-Marie 2002).  A maximum time at large of 11 years for tag returns of terminally molted mature male snow crab in the North Atlantic has been recorded since tagging started about 1993 (Fonseca, et al. 2008).  Fonseca, et al. (2008) estimated a maximum age of 7.8 years post terminal molt using data on dactal wear.

In recent years, the mean for the prior for natural mortality used in the eastern Bering Sea snow crab assessment was based on the assumption that longevity would be at least 20 years in an unfished population of snow crab, informed by the studies above.  Under negative exponential depletion, the 99th percentile corresponding to age 20 of an unexploited population corresponds to a natural mortality rate of 0.23.  Using Hoenig's (1983) method a natural mortality equal to 0.23 corresponds to a maximum age of 18 years.

In contrast to the implied natural mortalities from the methodology used above, Murphy et al. (2018) estimated time-varying natural mortality for eastern Bering Sea snow crab with a mean of 0.49 for females and 0.36 for males based on the output of state-space models fit to NMFS survey data. Further, natural mortality estimates produced from empirical analyses by Then et al. (2015) and Hamel (2015) using similar assumed maximum ages as the methodology above produced natural mortalities larger than 0.23 (\autoref{natM_empir}). Then et al. (2015) compared several major empirical estimation methods for M (including Hoenig's method) with an updated data set and found that maximum age was the best available predictor. A maximum age of 20 years corresponded to an M of ~0.315 in Then et al.'s analysis. Hamel (2015) developed priors in a similar manner to Then et al., but forced the regression of observed natural mortality onto maximum age through the intercept, which resulted in an M of ~0.27 for an assumed maximum age of 20 years.

```{r,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=F}

# format all the above into a tabular format

dat<-data.frame( c(0.277,0.315,0.365),
            c(0.19,0.212,0.257),
            c(0.194, 0.223, 0.261),
            c(0.235, 0.271, 0.318))

rownames(dat)<-c(23,20,17)
colnames(dat)<-c("Then","Hoenig (1983)","Hoenig (2013)","Hamel")

pander(t(dat),split.cells=20,caption="\\label{natM_empir} Empirical estimates of natural mortality (per year) for a range of methods over a range of assumed maximum ages (column header). These are empirical estimators, not output of any assessment model.")

```

In addition to the results of empirical estimates of M from updated methodologies and state-space modeling by Murphy et al. (2018), inspection of the survey data suggests that natural mortality for mature individuals is higher than assumed. A fraction of the mature population (which are assumed not to grow, given evidence for a terminal molt) are not selected in the fishery (e.g. sizes 50-80 mm; \autoref{natM_mature}). Consequently, all mortality observed is 'natural'. The collapse in recruitment in the 1990s can be used as an instrument to understand natural mortality for mature individuals. The last large recruitment enters these size classes in the mid- to late-1990s and numbers of crab in these size classes return to low levels in less than 5 years.

The median value of the priors used in this assessment are set equal to values resulting from assuming a maximum age of 20 years and applying Hamel's methodology (0.271). A standard error of 0.0054 was used for initial priors and was estimated using the 95% CI of +-1.7 years on maximum age estimates from dactal wear and tag return analysis in Fonseca, et al. (2008). Mortality events in 2018 and 2019 are estimated as additional mortality parameters applied by sex and maturity state to allow the model to fit recent population trends.

## Maturity

Maturity of females collected during the NMFS summer survey was determined by the shape of the abdomen, by the presence of brooded eggs, or egg remnants. Maturity for males was determined by chela height measurements, which were available most years starting from the 1989 survey (Otto 1998; \autoref{maturity_facet} & \autoref{maturity_facet_all}). Mature male biomass referenced throughout this document refers to a morphometrically mature male (i.e. large-clawed). A maturity curve for males was estimated using the average fraction mature based on chela height data and applied to years of survey data to estimate mature survey numbers that do not have chela height data available (see Richar and Foy, 2022 for details).

Bering Sea male snow crab appear to have a terminal molt to maturity based on hormone level data and findings from molt stage analysis via setagenesis (Tamone et al. 2005).  The models presented here assume a terminal molt for both males and females, which is supported by research on populations in the Bering Sea and the Atlantic Ocean (e.g. Dawe et al. 1991).

Mature male snow crab that do not molt may be important in reproduction.  Paul et al. (1995) found that old shell mature male Tanner crab out-competed new shell crab of the same size in breeding in a laboratory study.  Recently molted males did not breed even with no competition and may not breed until after ~100 days from molting (Paul et al. 1995).  Sainte-Marie et al. (2002) stated that only old shell males take part in mating for North Atlantic snow crab.

## Mating ratio and reproductive success

Bering Sea snow crab have historically been managed using morphometrically mature male biomass (MMB) as a proxy for reproductive potential. MMB is used as the currency for management because the fishery only retains large male crab, which are nearly 100% mature. Male snow crab are sperm conservers, using less than 4% of their sperm at each mating and females also can mate with more than one male. The amount of stored sperm and clutch fullness varies with sex ratio (Sainte-Marie 2002).  If mating with only one male is inadequate to fertilize a full clutch, then females would need to mate with more than one male, necessitating a sex ratio closer to 1:1 in the mature population, than if one male is assumed to be able to adequately fertilize multiple females. Although mature male biomass is currently the currency of management, some aspect of female reproduction is likely also an important indicator of reproductive potential of the stock.

 Clutch fullness is recorded for the females measured in the survey (see ESP; Fedewa et al., 2025). However, quantifying the reproductive potential of the female population from survey data can be difficult. For example, full clutches of unfertilized eggs may be extruded and appear normal to visual examination, and may be retained for several weeks or months by snow crab. Resorption of eggs may occur if not all eggs are extruded resulting in less than a full clutch.  Female snow crab at the time of the survey may have a full clutch of eggs that are unfertilized, resulting in overestimation of reproductive potential. Barren females may be a more obvious indication of low reproductive potential and increased in the early 1990s, decreased in the mid-1990s, then increased again in the late 1990s. The highest levels of barren females coincided with periods of high fishing mortality, but even then the proportion of barren females was low (see ESP; Fedewa et al., 2025). Biennial spawning is another confounding factor in determining the reproductive potential of snow crab. Laboratory analyses showed that female snow crab collected in waters colder than 1.5 degrees C from the Bering Sea spawn only every two years.

Further complicating the process of quantifying reproductive capacity, clutch fullness and fraction of unmated females may not account for the fraction of females that may have unfertilized eggs, since these cannot be detected by eye at the time of the survey.  The fraction of barren females observed in the survey may not be an accurate measure of fertilization success because females may retain unfertilized eggs for months after extrusion.  To examine this hypothesis, NMFS personnel sampled mature females from the Bering Sea in winter and held them in tanks until their eggs hatched in March of the same year (Rugolo et al. 2005).  All females then extruded a new clutch of eggs in the absence of males.  All eggs were retained until the crab were euthanized near the end of August.  Approximately 20% of the females had full clutches of unfertilized eggs.  The unfertilized eggs could not be distinguished from fertilized eggs by visual inspection at the time they were euthanized.  Indices of fertilized females based on the visual inspection method of assessing clutch fullness and percent unmated females may overestimate fertilized females.

## Growth

Several studies are available to estimate the growth per molt of male and female snow crab in the Bering Sea. These studies include:

1.  Transit study (2003); 14 crab
2.	Cooperative seasonality study; 6 crab
3.	Dutch harbor holding study; 9 crab
4.	NMFS Kodiak holding study held less than 30 days;  6 crab
5.  NMFS Kodiak holding study 2016; 5 crab
6.  NMFS Kodiak holding study 2017; 70 crab.
7.  BSFRF/NMFS holding study 2018; 4 crab.
8.  BSFRF/NMFS holding study 2021; 177 crab.

In the "Transit study", pre- and post-molt measurements of 14 male crab that molted soon after being captured were collected.  The crab were measured when shells were still soft because all died after molting, so measurements may be underestimates of post-molt width (L. Rugolo, pers. com.). The holding studies include only data for crab held less than 30 days because growth of crab held until the next spring's molting was much lower. Crab missing more than two limbs were excluded due to other studies showing lower growth. Crab from the seasonal study were excluded that were measured less than 3 days after molting due to difficulty in measuring soft crab accurately (L. Rugolo, pers. comm.). In general, growth of snow crab in the Bering Sea appears to be greater than growth of some North Atlantic snow crab stocks (Sainte-Marie 1995).  Crab in their first few years of life may molt more than once per year, however, the smallest crab included in the model are approximately 4 years old and would be expected to molt annually.

## Management history

<!-- TODO 2026: this section was a header-only stub in the 2025 reference Rmd; fill with the management-history narrative or fold into ADFG harvest strategy. -->

## ADFG harvest strategy

Before the year 2000, the Guideline Harvest Level (GHL) for retained crab only was a 58% harvest rate of the number of male crab over 101 mm CW estimated from the survey.  The minimum legal size limit for snow crab is 78 mm, however, the snow crab market generally only accepts crab greater than 101 mm.  In 2000, due to the decline in abundance and the declaration of the stock as overfished, the harvest rate for calculation of the GHL was reduced to 20% of male crab over 101 mm.  After 2000, a rebuilding strategy was developed based on simulations by Zheng et al. (2002) using survey biomass estimates. The realized retained catch often exceeded the GHL historically.

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADFG) harvest strategy since 2000 sets harvest rate based on estimated mature biomass. The harvest rate scales with the status of the population relative to a proxy for B~*MSY*~, which is calculated as the average total mature biomass at the time of the survey from 1983 to present and MSST is one half the B~*MSY*~ proxy.  The harvest rate begins at 0.10 when total mature biomass exceeds 50% MSST (230 million lbs) and increases linearly to 0.225 when biomass is equal to or greater than the B~*MSY*~ proxy (Zheng et al. 2002).

\begin{equation}
 u =
 \begin{cases}
 Bycatch  & if \frac{TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} \leq 0.25 \\[3ex]
 \frac {0.225 ( \frac {TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} - \alpha)}{1-\alpha}  & if 0.25 < \frac {TMB}{TMB_{MSY}} < 1 \\[3ex]
 0.225 & if TMB >TMB_{MSY}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}

Where *TMB* is the total mature biomass and TMB~*BMSY*~ is the *TMB* associated with maximum sustainable yield. The maximum retained catch is set as the product of the exploitation rate, *u*, calculated from the above control rule and survey mature male biomass.  If the retained catch in numbers is greater than 58% of the estimated number of new shell crab greater than 101 mm plus 25% of the old shell crab greater than 101 mm, the catch is capped at 58%.

## History of BMSY

Prior to adoption of Amendment 24, B~*MSY*~ was defined as the average total mature biomass (males and females) estimated from the survey for the years 1983 to 1997 (921.6 million lbs; NPFMC 1998) and MSST was defined as 50% of B~*MSY*~. Currently, the biological reference point for biomass is calculated using a spawning biomass per recruit proxy, B~*35%*~ (Clark, 1993). B~*35%*~ is the biomass at which spawning biomass per recruit is 35% of unfished levels and has been shown to provide close to maximum sustainable yield for a range of stock productivities (Clark, 1993). Consequently, it is an often used target when a stock recruit relationship is unknown or unreliable.  The range of years of recruitment used to calculate biomass reference points is from 1982 to the present assessment year, minus 1. However, recent analyses suggest SPR-based reference points do not provide a meaningful constraint on the snow crab fishery when the probability of having undergone terminal molt is specified to reflect observations in the survey. This is because a large fraction of the population matures (and ceases growing) at a size smaller than is harvested by the fishery.

## Fishery history

Snow crab were harvested in the Bering Sea by the Japanese from the 1960s until 1980 when the Magnuson Act prohibited foreign fishing. After the closure to foreign fleets, retained catches increased from relatively low levels in the early 1980s (e.g.  `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1982)$obs[1]),2)` kt during 1982) to historical highs in 1990s (retained catches during 1991, 1992, and 1998 were `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1991)$obs[1]),2)`, `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1992)$obs[1]),2)`, and `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1998)$obs[1]),2)` kt, respectively).  The stock was declared overfished in 1999 at which time retained catches dropped to levels similar to the early 1980s (e.g. `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2000)$obs[1]),2)` kt). Retained catches slowly increased after 1999 before dropping again in 2016. Total allowable catches were reduced with the collapse of the population in 2021, the fishery was closed for the first time in 2022, and the closure continued through 2023. A small fishery occurred in 2024. <!-- TODO 2026: extend to the 2025/26 fishery once characterized (ADFG retained ~4.1 kt in crab_year 2025). -->

Discard mortality from the directed fishery is the next largest source of mortality after retained catch and approximately tracks the retained catch. The highest estimated discard mortality occurred during 1990 at `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[2]),2)` kt which was `r round(100*as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[2])/ as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==1990)$obs[1]),2)`% of the retained catch during that year. Discard mortality in 2024 was `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2024)$obs[2]),2)` kt; the directed fishery was closed in 2022 and 2023, so no directed discards were recorded in those years. Non-directed mortality continues to be very small at `r round(as.numeric(filter(reslst$repsLst[[accepted_model]]$Catch_fit_summary,year==2024)$obs[4]),2)` kt in 2024.

Discard from the directed pot fishery has been estimated from observer data since 1992 and has ranged from 11-100% of the magnitude of retained catch by numbers. Discards reached 50-100% of the magnitude of retained catch in the lead up to the collapse after the 2018-2019 heatwave because of the large year class entering the population. Female discard catch has been very low compared to male discard catch and has not been a significant source of mortality. Discard mortality rates for the directed fishery are assumed to be 30%. Discard of snow crab in groundfish fisheries has been highest in the yellowfin sole trawl fishery, and decreases down through the flathead sole trawl fishery, Pacific cod bottom trawl fishery, rock sole trawl fishery, and the Pacific cod hook-and-line and pot fisheries, respectively (\autoref{bycatch}).  Bycatch in fisheries other than the groundfish trawl fishery has historically been relatively low. Discard mortality rates from non-directed fisheries are assumed to be 80%. Size frequency data and catch per pot have been collected by observers on snow crab fishery vessels since 1992.  Observer coverage has been 10% on catcher vessels larger than 125 ft (since 2001), and 100% coverage on catcher processors (since 1992).

Several modifications to pot gear have been introduced to reduce bycatch mortality.  In the 1978/79 season, escape panels were required on pots used in the snow crab fishery to prevent ghost fishing.  Escape panels consist of an opening with one-half the perimeter of the tunnel eye laced with untreated cotton twine.  The size of the cotton laced panel was increased in 1991 to at least 18 inches in length.  No escape mechanisms for undersized crab were required until the 1997 season when at least one-third of one vertical surface of pots had to contain not less than 5 inches stretched mesh webbing or have no less than four circular rings of no less than 3 3/4 inches inside diameter.  In the 2001 season the escapement provisions for undersized crab was increased to at least eight escape rings of no less than 4 inches placed within one mesh measurement from the bottom of the pot, with four escape rings on each side of the two sides of a four-sided pot, or one-half of one side of the pot must have a side panel composed of not less than 5 1/4 inch stretched mesh webbing.

# D. Data

Updated time series of survey indices and size compositions were calculated from data downloaded from the AKFIN database. Bycatch data (biomass and size composition) were updated for the most recent year from the AKFIN database. Retained, total, and discarded catch (in numbers and biomass) and size composition data for each of these data sources were updated for the most recent year based on files provided by the State of Alaska.

## Catch data

Catch data and size composition of retained crab from the directed snow crab pot fishery from survey year 1982 to 2025 were used in this analysis (\autoref{obscatch}). Time series of discarded catch from the directed fishery are fit, but size composition data are for total catch. The discard male catch was estimated for survey years 1982 to 1991 in the model using the estimated fishery selectivities based on the observer data for the period of survey year 1992 to 2025. The discards prior to 1992 may be underestimated due to the lack of escape mechanisms for undersized crab in the pots before 1997. See \autoref{datayears} for a summary of catch data range.

## Survey biomass and size composition data
Estimates of of the numbers of crab by sex and size from the annual eastern Bering Sea (EBS) bottom trawl survey conducted by NMFS (e.g. \autoref{n_at_len} & \autoref{n_at_len_f}; see Lang et al., 2018 for materials and methods; see the most recent tech memo for detailed description) are used to calculate the primary indices of abundance used in this assessment. Additional survey stations were added in 1989, which could alter the interpretation of catchability coefficient for the survey. Consequently, survey selectivity has been historically modeled in two 'eras' in the assessment (1982-1988, 1989-present). All survey data in this assessment used measured net widths instead of the fixed 50 ft net width based on Chilton et al.'s (2009) survey estimates. Carapace width and shell conditions were measured and reported for snow crab caught in the survey.

Mature male size composition data were calculated by multiplying the total numbers at length for new shell male crab by a vector of observed proportion of mature males at length. All old shell crab of both sexes were assumed to be mature.  New shell crab were demarcated as any crab with shell condition index <= 2. The biomass of new and old shell mature individuals was calculated by multiplying the vector of numbers at length by weight at length. These vectors were then summed by sex to provide the input for assessment (\autoref{obsbio}).  Input sample sizes are specified as 100 for both sexes and maturity states for all years of survey size composition data.

## Spatial distribution of survey abundance and catch
Snow crab are distributed widely over the eastern Bering Sea shelf, but their density and the extent of their distribution has changed over time (see tech memo). Spatial gradients exist in the survey data by maturity and size for both sexes.  For example, larger males have been more prevalent on the southwest portion of the shelf while smaller males have been more prevalent on the northern portion of the shelf. Centroids of mature female abundance early in the history of the survey were farther south, but moved north during the 1990s. Since the late 1990s and early 2000s, the centroids moved south again, but not to the extent seen in the early 1980s. This phenomenon was mirrored in centroids of abundance for large males.

Fishing effort has generally been south of 58.5 N, even when ice cover did not restrict the fishery moving farther north (\autoref{effort_sp} & \autoref{recent_eff}).  This is possibly due to the proximity to port and practical constraints of meeting delivery schedules. Unstandardized CPUE (hereafter just 'CPUE') in the fishery has varied over time and an increase in average CPUE occurred after rationalization (\autoref{year_cpue}).  The change in CPUE in a given spatial area within a season can reflect the impact of the fishery on the population in that area. Declines in CPUE can be seen by spatial area over time within a season (\autoref{cpue_trend}).

The observed distribution of large males during the summer survey and the fishery catch have historically differed, and the origin of this difference is unknown. It is possible that crab move between the fishery and the survey, but it is also possible that fishers do not target all portions of the distribution of large male crab equally. The underlying explanation of this phenomenon could hold implications for relative exploitation rates spatially and it has been suggested that high exploitation rates in the southern portion of the snow crab range may have resulted in a northward shift in snow crab distribution (Orensanz, 2004). Snow crab larvae likely drift north and east after hatching in spring. Snow crab appear to move south and west as they grow (Parada et al., 2010); however, little tagging data exists to fully characterize the ontogenetic or annual migration patterns of this stock (Murphy et al. 2010).

## Experimental study of survey selectivity

The Bering Sea Fisheries Research Foundation (BSFRF) has conducted supplementary surveys in the Bering Sea in which snow crab were caught during 2009, 2010, 2016, 2017, and 2018.  The location and extent of these surveys varied over the years as the survey goals changed. In 2009, the survey consisted of 108 tows around 27 survey stations and the goal was to improve understanding snow crab densities and the selectivity of NMFS survey gear (\autoref{bsfrfmap}). Abundances estimated by the industry surveys were generally higher than the NMFS estimates, which suggests that the catchability of the NMFS survey gear is less than 1.

In 2016, 2017, and 2018, snow crab were not the focus of the BSFRF surveys, but were still caught in the BSFRF gear. Comparing the ratio of the number of crab caught at length in the BSFRF gear (which is assumed to have a catchability/selectivity of 1 over all size classes) to the number of crab caught at length within the same area in the NMFS survey gear (which is assumed to have a catchability/selectivity <= to 1 for at least some of the size classes) can provide an empirical estimate of catchability/selectivity (\autoref{bsfrf_sel}). Empirical estimates of catchability/selectivity vary by year and size class across the different BSFRF data sets (\autoref{bsfrf_sel_all} & \autoref{emp_sel}). The number of snow crab used to develop estimates of numbers at length likely contribute to these differences among years (\autoref{bsfrf_sampN}), but other factors may also influence catchability/selectivity at size of the NMFS survey gear (e.g. Somerton et al. 2013 show substrate type can influence selectivity). GAMs fit to the empirical estimates of selectivity are used are priors on estimated selectivity in the currently used assessment model. The standard errors from the GAMs are input as weighting factors for each prior of selectivity at size and sex derived from the BSFRF data.

# E. Analytic approach


## Model description

The Generalized Model for Assessing Crustacean Stocks (GMACS) was adopted as the assessment platform for snow crab in 2022 after a demonstration that GMACS could effectively reproduce the dynamics of the status quo model and offered structural improvements. GMACS is an integrated, size-structured model developed using automatic differentiation software developed as a set of libraries under C++ (ADModel Builder).  ADModel Builder can estimate a large number of parameters in a non-linear model using automatic differentiation software extended from Greiwank and Corliss (1991) and developed into C++ class libraries.  GMACS version 2.20.34 was used for the author-preferred software after the January 2026 CPT.

The snow crab population dynamics model tracks the number of crab of sex *s*,  maturity state *m*, during year *y* at width *w*, N~*s,m,y,w*~. A terminal molt was modeled in which crab move from an immature to a mature state, after which no further molting occurred. The mid-points of the size bins tracked in the model spanned from 27.5 to 132.5 mm carapace width, with 5 mm size classes. The number of estimated parameters differs among the models: 407 in `Model 25`, `Model 25.2c` and `Model 25.2e`, 412 in `Model 25.2e (new data)`, 386 in `Model 25.2e (2019 data)`, and 234 in `Model 26.1`. Parameters estimated within the assessment included those associated with the population processes recruitment, growth, natural mortality (subject to an informative prior and two years of additional 'mortality events' estimated in 2018 and 2019), fishing mortality, selectivity (fisheries and survey), and catchability. The yearly probability of undergoing terminal molt, weight at size, discard mortality, bycatch mortality, variance in growth increment, and parameters associated with proportion of recruitment allocated to size bin were estimated outside of the model or specified. See the GMACS repo linked at the end of this document to peruse the control files that specify the populations dynamics.

A lognormal distribution was assumed for all catch and index time-series, while a robust multinomial was assumed for all size composition data. No likelihood weights were used in the assessment.

```{r jitter-setup, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Jitter outputs, written by 05_run_jitter.R. Every jitter value quoted in this
# document is pulled from this object at knit time so the text cannot drift
# from the runs. Absent runs yield NA and a visible note, never a plausible
# placeholder.
jit_path <- "Models/rda_jitter.RData"
jit_have <- file.exists(jit_path)
if (jit_have) load(jit_path)          # -> `jitter`: results / summary / modes / attribution / manifest

jit_sum <- if (jit_have) jitter$summary   else NULL
jit_res <- if (jit_have) jitter$results   else NULL
jit_man <- if (jit_have) jitter$manifest  else NULL

.js <- function(field, default = NA) {          # NA-safe accessor on the summary row
  if (!jit_have || !field %in% names(jit_sum)) return(default)
  jit_sum[[field]][1]
}
jit_fmt <- function(x, d = 2) if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0 || is.na(x)) "NA" else
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = "")

jit_n         <- .js("n_runs")
jit_sd        <- .js("jitter_sd")

A 'jittering' approach has been historically used to explore the impact of different starting values on the assessment output (Turnock, 2016). Parameter values were jittered based on a normal distribution centered on one with a standard deviation of `r jit_fmt(jit_sd, 2)` that was then translated to the parameter space defined by the initial value and its bounds. `r if (jit_have) sprintf("%s jitters were run for the author-recommended model (Table \\@ref(tab:model-overview)); each run was started from an independently perturbed parameter vector and re-fit to convergence.", jit_n)` Each jitter run used an explicitly recorded random seed, so the analysis is exactly reproducible; the seed used by every run is stored alongside its results. The September 2026 analysis jitters the single author-recommended model -- confirm this is the intended scope before the document goes to the CPT.]]

## Model selection and evaluation
Models were evaluated based on their fit to the data, evidence of non-convergence, the credibility of the estimated population processes, and the strength of the influence of the assumptions of the model on the outcomes of the assessment. Note that for some of the model scenarios, data inputs are different and, therefore, model fits are not directly comparable.

### Model summaries

The key assumptions of these models include: 

* the probability of terminally molting at size varies over time and size and is specified as fixed inputs to the model based on observations from the survey data

* survey selectivity is estimated by era (1982-88; 1989-present) and sex as a non-parametric curve subject to priors based on the BSFRF survey efficiency experiment data

* growth is a linear function of pre-molt carapace width with a specified variability around post-molt size

* all immature crab molt

* natural mortality is estimated by sex and maturity state with additional mortality events estimated in 2018 and 2019 and subject to a prior based on an assumed longevity of 20 years

* total and retained fishery selectivity are estimated logistic curves

* all non-directed bycatch (e.g. snow crab caught in the Tanner crab fishery or crab caught in the non-pelagic trawl fisheries) is lumped into a single 'fishery' for which a single selectivity is estimated; these removals are recorded for both sexes combined, so in the male-only sensitivity they are fit by the male population alone and the bycatch fishing mortality estimated for males is correspondingly inflated (the affected removals average 0.48 kt against a mean retained catch of 37.1 kt, and the fit to the series is essentially unchanged)

* recruitment is estimated separately for females and males and is allocated in the first 3 size bins; the male-only sensitivity estimates male recruitment only


### Model scenarios

A total of `r n_models` models were explored (Table \@ref(tab:model-overview)). All models share the same structural assumptions described above and differ only in the version of GMACs, their data inputs, specification of the maturity ogive, and the definition of the plus group. The naming convention reflects an additive series of changes layered onto the September 2025 model (`Model 25`). 

The base ('rolled forward') model:

* **Model 25** -- the September 2025 author-recommended model, included for reference only. No data are updated and no structural changes are made. It was fitted under an earlier version of GMACS and is reported as originally fitted.

Models carried forward from the May 2026 assessment:

* **Model 25.2c** -- the model accepted by the CPT in May 2026. `Model 25` updated to GMACS 2.20.34, with the total-male size composition corrected and the plus group enlarged to include all crab greater than 135 mm carapace width, and with the molting probability controls replaced by the array produced by the new maturity workflow developed by the Kodiak lab (E. Ryznar, in prep). That workflow fits an `sdmTMB` spatiotemporal model to chela-based maturity classifications to produce a smoothed probability of being mature at size and location, integrated to a population-level annual ogive; the updated series shows a weaker temporal trend in the probability of terminal molt at intermediate sizes. Data end in 2024, as in May.

* **Model 25.2e** -- as `Model 25.2c`, but with the size-composition bin convention changed so that a crab falling exactly on a 5 mm cutoff is assigned to the upper bin, and with a transcription error in the growth data corrected (a 26.3 mm crab's molt increment recorded as 73 mm where the specimen master gives 7.3 mm). Data end in 2024. Presented to isolate the effect of each correction against the May baseline.

The September 2026 models:

* **Model 25.2e (new data)** -- the author-recommended model. The `Model 25.2e` configuration advanced to end year 2025, so that the fishery data run through the 2025/26 season and the survey data through the 2026 summer survey. The data change; the model does not.

* **Model 25.2e (2019 data)** -- the same configuration with all data truncated to 2019, so that the fishery data end with the 2019/20 season and the survey with the 2019 summer survey. Requested by the CPT in May 2026 to test whether the convergence problems originate in estimating recruitment following the 2018-19 collapse and across the 2020 survey gap. The estimated parameter count is 386.

Sensitivity to the female data and dynamics:

* **Model 26.1** -- `Model 25.2e (new data)` with the female population removed entirely rather than merely down-weighted. The number of sexes is set to one, which removes the female size compositions, the female survey indices, the female discard catch, and the female growth observations from the data, and removes the female recruitment, natural mortality, growth, and selectivity parameters from the model. The estimated parameter count falls from 412 to 234. Fixing the female estimation phases alone would not accomplish this: a combined-sex catch observation is predicted by summing over both sexes, and the recruitment scale and deviations are not sex-specific, so the female population would continue to influence fishing mortality and recruitment. The non-directed bycatch is recorded for both sexes combined and is therefore fit by the male population alone in this run, as noted among the assumptions above. This is the only model presented here that differs structurally from `Model 25.2e`, which is why it takes a new number rather than a parenthetical. Requested by the CPT in May 2026 and presented as a sensitivity only; it is not proposed for specification unless the CPT selects it in September.

The May 2026 preliminary assessment presented a bracket of fourteen candidate models exploring three axes of uncertainty: the treatment of *Chionoecetes* hybrids, the new maturity workflow, and a set of attempts to improve convergence by correcting the total-male composition, expanding the plus group, and adding an immature survey index. That bracket is not repeated here. The CPT and SSC concluded that hybrid catch and survey data should not be included in the assessment model at this time, and agreed that the immature survey index should not be treated as a convergence fix, so neither the hybrid nor the immature-index candidates are carried forward. The composition correction and the expanded plus group, which the SSC supported as clear technical improvements, are incorporated in every model presented above. The full May bracket and its results remain available in the May 2026 preliminary assessment document.

Time series of data used in the assessment are visualized in (Figures \@ref(fig:indexdataplots), \@ref(fig:catchdataplots), \@ref(fig:compdataplots)). The sentence that stood here reported that the maturity and hybrid treatments led to small differences in male survey biomass, and cited a figure comparing the May hybrid and immature-index candidates; both that figure and those models are out of the September set, so the claim and its cross-reference have been removed rather than left pointing at nothing. ## Results
### Model convergence and comparison
The 2026 groundfish stock assessment guidelines set the convergence standard applied here: Newton steps taken with the inverse Hessian to reduce the maximum gradient below 1e-05, which the guidelines describe as stronger evidence of convergence than a maximum gradient or an invertible Hessian alone, while noting that it does not diagnose a local minimum. All `r n_models` models presented here inverted their Hessians (Table \@ref(tab:max-grad)). Where a fit did not initially meet the conventional convergence threshold of a maximum absolute gradient < 0.001, the solution was polished with Newton steps taken using the inverse Hessian, which reduces the gradient without moving the fit: across the models it changed the objective function by no more than 4 x 10^-7^ and the reference points by less than 1 part in 10^7^. `Model 25`, which was fitted under an earlier version of GMACS and cannot be re-run with the current executable, is reported as originally fitted. Likelihood components by category for each candidate model are summarized in Table \@ref(tab:like-index-tot), \@ref(tab:like-comp-tot), and \@ref(tab:like-other-tot).

A zero gradient should not be read as evidence that the parameters are well determined. It states that the fit sits at a stationary point of the likelihood, not that the likelihood is sharply peaked there, and it says nothing about how many other such points exist. The jitter analysis below speaks to the second question, and the near-zero Hessian eigenvalues discussed there to the first.

The practical cost of the multiple optima is visible in `Model 25.2c`. The jitter analysis located a solution 1.27 negative log-likelihood units better than the fit obtained from the model's own starting values, a difference that would ordinarily be considered small. Adopting it moved B~MSY~ by less than one percent, but moved the total OFL from 50.27 to 43.83 kt, a change of approximately 13 percent. The choice among solutions that the data separate only weakly therefore carries more consequence for the management quantity than several of the structural choices examined in this assessment.

Total OFL across the runs ranged from %s to %s kt and mature male biomass in %s from %s to %s kt, which is the residual spread within one optimum rather than a separation between optima.", jit_fmt(jit_ofl_min,2), jit_fmt(jit_ofl_max,2), jit_fmt(jit_term_yr,0), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_min,1), jit_fmt(jit_mmb_max,1))`

`r if (jit_have && jit_improve > 0.001 && jit_promoted) sprintf("One jitter run found a better fit than the starting solution, improving the negative log likelihood by %s units. Following the convention used in the 2025 assessment, that run was adopted as the reported model and re-fit with the Hessian; all quantities in this document derive from it. The provenance of that fit, including its random seed, is recorded with the model.", jit_fmt(jit_improve,3))`
`r if (jit_have && jit_improve > 0.001 && !jit_promoted) sprintf("One jitter run found a better fit than the reported model, improving the negative log likelihood by %s units. It has not been adopted. [[author: the 2025 assessment reported the lowest-likelihood run of 100 jitters; decide whether to do so here.]]", jit_fmt(jit_improve,3))`
`r if (jit_have && jit_improve <= 0.001) "No jitter run improved materially on the reported fit, which supports the reported solution being the global optimum rather than a local one."`

Identifying which parameters differ between the clouds, rather than only observing that the clouds exist, was requested by the SSC and is intended to direct the structural work needed to resolve the multiple optima.")` [[author: interpret the attribution result -- which processes the separating parameters belong to, and what that implies for the structural changes to evaluate before the next cycle.]]

Removing the female population improves the numerical behavior of the model. `Model 26.1` estimates 234 parameters against 412 for `Model 25.2e (new data)`. Its accepted fit attains a maximum absolute gradient of zero to reported precision after Newton polishing, and a Hessian markedly better conditioned than that of `Model 25.2e (new data)` (condition number 3.3e05 against 1.4e06, smallest eigenvalue 120 against 35), with no non-positive eigenvalues. Jittering the male-only model over 100 runs reached the best-fitting mode in 25.3% of the runs that reached an optimum, against 5.1% for `Model 25.2e (new data)`; the multimodality that has characterized this assessment is therefore reduced but not removed by dropping the females. The retrospective pattern is also smaller: Mohn's rho for mature male biomass is -0.09, or -0.08 when the terminal survey year is withheld, against -0.11 for `Model 25.2e (new data)`, and both remain inside the Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015) bounds. The terminal-year recruitment artifact is substantially reduced, with Mohn's rho for male recruitment falling from approximately 8 to 0.7. This is consistent with the expectation that removing the females reduces the confounding among growth, natural mortality, and selectivity. Dropping the females also lowers the reference points: $B_{MSY}$ falls from 144.97 to 131.34 kt and the total-catch OFL from 85.65 to 77.00 kt, with terminal mature male biomass falling from 141.53 to 115.90 kt (Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)).

```{r retro-setup, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

.rd <- function(f) {

  if (file.exists(p)) read.csv(p, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) else NULL
}
retro_rho  <- .rd("mohns_rho.csv")
retro_rel  <- .rd("retro_peel_relative.csv")
retro_diag <- .rd("retro_diagnostics.csv")
# The retrospective reports MMB and recruitment only. There is no
# retro_refpoints.csv: GMACS does not compute reference points for a peeled run
# (gmacsbase.TPL 2.20.34 gates both call sites on nyrRetroNo == 0, :5478 and
# :13625), so every peel returns them as exactly 0. Confirmed 2026-08-27; the
# peels run WITH the Hessian, so this was never a -nohess problem. The terminal

#
# NOT read here: retro/prj_growth_year_diagnostic.csv. It is a developer
# diagnostic, not an assessment result, and its BMSY = OFL = 0 columns are that
# same peel behavior. Nothing in the SAFE should be able to reach those zeros.

retro_have <- !is.null(retro_rho)

# convenience accessors; return NA (not an error) when the runs are absent
.rho <- function(mode, quantity) {
  if (!retro_have) return(NA_real_)
  v <- retro_rho$mohns_rho[retro_rho$mode == mode & retro_rho$quantity == quantity]

}

The guidelines also ask whether any parameters were inestimable or reached their bounds. In the accepted fit no parameter reached a bound and the Hessian is well conditioned: its smallest eigenvalue is 34.6 and none is non-positive. Twenty-four of the 545 estimated quantities have a standard error larger than the absolute value of the estimate. Sixteen of those are estimated within 0.1 of zero -- recruitment and fishing mortality deviations and selectivity offsets, where a large ratio is arithmetic rather than diagnostic. The remainder are three recruitment deviations, three recruitment proportion parameters, a fishing mortality deviation, and `M_pars_est[2]`, estimated at 0.33 with a standard error of 0.59.

That is a property of this fit and not of the model. In cold starts the model can settle in an optimum where the second natural-mortality block for immature females, `M_pars_est[15]`, is unidentified: it drifts toward its upper bound of 10 with a standard error of order 5 x 10^3^, the smallest Hessian eigenvalue falls to 1.1 x 10^-6^ against a next-smallest of 19.8, and the likelihood acquires a single flat direction along which a cold start lands wherever floating-point noise takes it. In the accepted fit that same parameter is estimated at 1.83 with a standard error of 0.58, consistent with its block-one counterpart at 1.80, and the flat direction is absent. Whether an exponential time-varying natural mortality block on immature females is identifiable from these data at all is a question for the Plan Team; the alternative is to fix it, as the corresponding rows for the other sex and maturity combinations already are.

### Retrospective analysis
`r if (!retro_have) "*Retrospective results not yet generated; run 06_run_retrospective.R to produce them.*"`

Retrospective analyses were performed by sequentially removing the terminal year of data from the model, re-fitting, and comparing the resulting time series of estimated mature male biomass with the estimates from the model fit to the full data set. A retrospective pattern is a consistent directional change in an assessment estimate for a given year as additional years of data are added. `r if (retro_have) sprintf("Peels of one through %d years were run, giving terminal years from %d back to %d.", retro_npeel, retro_yr1, retro_yrN)`

Mohn's $\rho$ is reported here as the mean across peels of the relative difference between each peel's terminal-year estimate and the estimate for that same year from the model fit to all of the data,

$$\rho = \frac{1}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\frac{X_{T_p,\,p}-X_{T_p,\,0}}{X_{T_p,\,0}},$$

where $T_p$ is the terminal year of peel $p$ and $X_{\cdot,0}$ is the unpeeled fit. A positive $\rho$ therefore means the peels sit *above* the full model, i.e. that terminal biomass is revised downward as data accumulate. Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015) suggest that $\rho$ outside $[-0.22,\,0.30]$ for a short-lived stock indicates a retrospective pattern worth reporting.

Two retrospectives are presented. The **standard** retrospective removes the last $p$ years of all data streams. The **dropped-terminal-survey** retrospective additionally withholds the most recent survey year, which isolates the leverage of the single most recent survey observation on the terminal estimate. This distinction matters for this stock because, under the crab-year convention, an assessment with end year $N$ is fit to the summer survey from year $N+1$, so the terminal MMB estimate rests heavily on one very recent survey point.

`r if (retro_have) sprintf("For mature male biomass, the standard retrospective gave Mohn's $\\rho$ = %s and the dropped-terminal-survey retrospective gave $\\rho$ = %s (Table \\@ref(tab:retro-rho), Figures \\@ref(fig:retro-mmb) and \\@ref(fig:retro-drop-survey)). Male recruitment gave $\\rho$ = %s.", .fmt(.rho("standard","mature_male_biomass")), .fmt(.rho("drop_survey","mature_male_biomass")), .fmt(.rho("standard","recruitment_male")))`

Management quantities are not recomputed for each peel. GMACS calculates reference points only when the retrospective peel count is zero (`gmacsbase.TPL` 2.20.34 gates both call sites on `nyrRetroNo == 0`), so every peeled run returns $B_{MSY}$, $B/B_{MSY}$ and the OFL as exactly zero rather than as estimates. This is a property of GMACS and not of the runs presented here -- the peels were fit with the Hessian -- and it applies equally to the 2025 assessment. The retrospective therefore characterizes mature male biomass and recruitment only, and the movement in the management advice itself under each peel cannot be read from it. [[author: if the CPT wants the advice-level retrospective for a scientific-uncertainty buffer, it needs peel-by-peel reference points computed outside GMACS.]]

<!-- >>> REVIEW: once the peels are final, characterize the DIRECTION and PRACTICAL
     SIGNIFICANCE of the pattern here in words (the numbers above are pulled
     automatically, but the interpretation is an author judgement). Also state
     whether the retrospective motivates any change to the ABC buffer. -->

Each peel was re-fit with the Hessian rather than being seeded from the full model's variance estimates. The projection file was left unmodified; GMACS shifts its reference-point averaging windows back by the number of peeled years internally.

### Historical analysis

The retrospective analysis above withholds data from a single model. A historical analysis asks a different question: how the perception of the stock has changed across successive assessments accepted for management. Figure \@ref(fig:historical-mmb) shows estimated mature male biomass at mating as each assessment from 2016 to 2025 saw it.

The revisions are large, and they are much larger than the within-model retrospective pattern. The clearest case is the collapse itself. The 2020 assessment put mature male biomass at the time of the survey in 2020 at 486.5 kt; the 2021 assessment, with the 2021 survey in hand, revised that same year to 40.95 kt, a downward revision of 92 percent. The revision then reversed: the 2022 assessment estimated 2020 biomass at mating at 19.1 kt, and the 2023 assessment revised the same year to 205.4 kt, an order-of-magnitude increase in the opposite direction. Terminal-year estimates across the ten vintages range from 26.7 kt (2021 assessment) to 207.2 kt (2020 assessment).

[[author: the guidelines ask for the cause of any obvious differences, and that cause cannot be established from the material in this repository -- `data/historical/` holds the published time series but not the configurations that produced them. The candidates worth checking against the 2021--2023 assessment documents are the treatment of the 2018--19 mortality event, changes in the maturity input, and any change in the initialisation. Note that the time-varying probability of terminal molt is not itself new this cycle; what changed for 2026 is the workflow producing it.]]

The practical consequence for management advice is that terminal-year mature male biomass in this assessment has historically been revised by considerably more than the within-model retrospective analysis implies, and in both directions. [[author: the guidelines ask for uncertainty intervals on the vintages. The published series in `data/historical/` carry point estimates only, so the figure shows no intervals; either recover the intervals from the archived assessments or state here that they were not available.]]
