### Model fits
Fits to the survey indices of mature biomass were broadly similar across the models (Figure \@ref(fig:mmbfits)). The two models that incorporate the 2026 NMFS summer survey, `Model 25.2e (new data)` and `Model 26.1`, continue to have difficulty fitting the terminal year of female biomass in the two-sex case. Inputting a yearly varying probability of terminal molt from the new maturity workflow (`Models 25.2`) shifts the estimated population dynamics modestly but does not resolve the female terminal-year fit (Figure \@ref(fig:mmbfits)).

[[author: this paragraph described the hybrid-survey and `imm_surv` candidates, which are not in the September set -- the CPT and SSC advised against both in May and June 2026. Replace with a comparison across the six models actually presented, or drop it.]]

Fits to the non-directed fishery catches were good for all models (Figure \@ref(fig:catchfits)). Fits to the directed-fishery retained catch were also good across the model set. [[author: a sentence here compared discard fits in the hybrid-fishery models, which are not in the September set. Removed rather than left describing models the document does not present. The underlying observation -- that ADF&G reported roughly 18 kt of legal-male hybrid catch in 1997, with hybrid identification quality decreasing further back in the time series -- is still recorded in Table \@ref(tab:obscatch) and may be worth keeping somewhere.]] The models accommodate the additional discards primarily through changes in estimated discard fishing mortality rather than through major changes in selectivity.

Differences among models in the fits to size composition data for retained catch in the directed fishery are small (size composition figures, below). Fits to the total size composition data from the directed fishery differ noticeably between the standard and the hybrid-fishery models, particularly for the larger size bins where hybrids are most prevalent. No visually discernible differences among models existed for female discards from the directed fishery. Fits to the non-directed fishery had some of the largest misfits of all data sources (particularly for male data), but this is unsurprising given a single estimated selectivity curve and changes in fishery behavior over time. Sample sizes are assumed to be 100 for all composition data except for female discards in 2021, 2024 and 2025 (sample size = 10).

Fits to the survey size composition data were broadly similar across models in most years (size composition figures, below). The plus-group change (extending the plus group to all crab > 135 mm) makes a small visual difference for retained males but improves the runtime of the model substantially. All models had difficulty fitting the size composition data for immature females in 2009 and 2019, which could suggest some unmodeled size-based mortality or time-varying probability of terminal molt. Estimates of mean growth are shown in Figure \@ref(fig:growthfits).

### Estimated population processes
The estimated abundance of commercially preferred male crab (>=101 mm carapace width) varied among models (Figure \@ref(fig:obs-101-vs-pred)). The early years during which differences in survey selectivity occurred were particularly different. All models agreed that the abundance in recent years has been the lowest in the time series (Figure \@ref(fig:obs-101-vs-pred-bio)). The estimates of the most recent era of survey selectivity were similar across models for both sexes (Figure \@ref(fig:select-prior)).

Estimated fisheries selectivities were similar across models (Figure \@ref(fig:predselectfish)). Estimated fully-selected fishing mortality for the directed fishery was highly variable and relatively high for most of the fishery history (Figure \@ref(fig:predfmort)). The total fishery selectivity curve is shifted far to the right, so only the largest crab experience the fully-selected fishing mortality. 

The probability of undergoing terminal molt is input as data (Figure \@ref(fig:predmat)); the status quo workflow produces a strong increasing trend through time at intermediate sizes (e.g., at 77 mm the probability rose from ~0.2 in the early 1990s to ~0.5 after 2010), while [[VERIFY: this comparison of the two maturity workflows -- the quoted probabilities at 77 mm and the characterisation of one trend as strong and the other as weak -- could not be reproduced from the terminal-molt arrays in the control files. Check it against the workflow output directly before this goes out.]] the new maturity workflow produces a much weaker temporal trend (~0.35--0.45 throughout the time series). The new workflow uses a spatiotemporal `sdmTMB` model fit to chela-based maturity classifications and borrows information across years and locations for size bins with sparse chela data; it does not extrapolate the predicted spatial probability surface beyond stations with measured crab.

Trends in recruitment were very similar across models for the early time series, with some variability in scale and differences in timing between the sexes (Figure \@ref(fig:recruits)). Differences in estimated recruitment in the most recent years were observed among models for males and contribute to differences in OFLs across the model set.

Base estimates of natural mortality for mature animals of both sexes were broadly similar across the models presented (Figure \@ref(fig:nat-m), Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)). All models estimated additional mortality events that removed a large fraction of crab by sex and maturity state, except for mature females, at some point during the marine heatwave of 2018--19. In every model the immature-female natural mortality deviation for the second event block is poorly determined, with a standard error far larger than the estimate itself; whether that parameter should be fixed rather than estimated is discussed under model convergence. [[author: the May document also reported an extreme immature-female M in one of the hybrid candidates; those models are not carried forward, so that observation has been removed rather than restated.]]

### MMB and management quantities
Estimated mature male biomass time series had similar trends across models but differed in scale (Figure \@ref(fig:predmmb)). Estimates of $B_{MSY}$, current MMB relative to $B_{MSY}$, $F_{MSY}$, $F_{OFL}$ and the Tier 3 OFL are summarized in Table \@ref(tab:stepchange). Across the models presented, the $B_{MSY}$ proxy ranged from 131.3 to 180.1 kt and terminal mature male biomass from 86.9 to 141.5 kt. The three models whose data end in 2024 place the stock below its $B_{MSY}$ proxy (status 0.81 to 0.96), while the two carrying the 2025 fishery and 2026 survey place it above (status 1.23 and 1.32); the additional year of data, rather than any structural change, accounts for that difference.

[[author: a paragraph comparing the hybrid candidates' $B_{MSY}$ proxies stood here. Those models are not carried forward and the paragraph has been removed; the audit-trail note in Section E records that hybrids were evaluated in May and excluded on CPT and SSC advice.]]

# F. Calculation of the OFL
## Methodology for OFL 
### Tier 3
Historically, the tier 3 OFL was calculated using proxies for biomass and fishing mortality reference points and a sloped control rule. Proxies for biomass and fishing mortality reference points were calculated using spawning-biomass-per-recruit methods (e.g. Clark, 1991). After fitting the assessment model to the data and estimating population parameters, the model was projected forward 100 years using the estimated parameters under no exploitation and constant recruitment to determine 'unfished' mature male biomass-per-recruit. Projections were repeated in which the bisection method was used to identify a fishing mortality that reduced the mature male biomass-per-recruit to 35% of the unfished level (i.e. F~35%~ and B~35%~). Calculations of F~*35%*~ were made under the assumption that bycatch fishing mortality was equal to the estimated average value over the last 10 years. 

Calculated values of F~35%~ and B~35%~ were used in conjunction with a Tier 3 control rule to adjust the proportion of F~35%~ that is applied to the stock based on the status of the population relative to B~35%~ (Amendment 24, NMFS). To determine the F~OFL~, the population is projected to the time of fishing for the upcoming fishery under no fishing. If the MMB at that time exceeds 25% of B~35%~, a fishery can occur and the F~OFL~ is calculated as:

$$\begin{equation}
F_{OFL} =
\begin{cases}
Bycatch  & if \frac{MMB}{B_{35}} \leq 0.25 \\[3ex]
\frac {F_{35} ( \frac {MMB}{B_{35}} - \alpha)}{1-\alpha}  & if 0.25 < \frac {MMB}{B_{35}} < 1 \\[3ex]
F_{35} & if MMB > B_{35}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}$$

Where MMB is the projected morphometrically mature male biomass in the current survey year after fishing at the F~*OFL*~, B~*35%*~ is the mature male biomass at the time of mating resulting from fishing at F~*35%*~, F~*35%*~ is the fishing mortality that reduces the morphometrically mature male biomass per recruit to 35% of unfished levels, and $\alpha$ determines the slope of the descending limb of the harvest control rule (set to 0.1 here).

Calculated total Tier 3 OFLs across the models presented ranged from 43.8 to 147.3 kt (Table \@ref(tab:stepchange)). For reference, the observed survey biomass of morphometrically mature males in 2025 was `r .f(survey_morph_2025, 1)` kt and of preferred males (> 101 mm) `r .f(survey_pref_2025, 1)` kt. Taking `Model 25.2c`, the model accepted in May, as the comparison baseline at 43.8 kt: correcting the size-composition bin convention and the growth transcription error (`Model 25.2e`) lowered the $B_{MSY}$ proxy from 172.7 to 158.7 kt and raised the OFL to 53.7 kt; adding the 2025 fishery and 2026 survey (`Model 25.2e (new data)`) lowered the proxy further to 145.0 kt, raised status above one, and raised the OFL to 85.6 kt. The male-only sensitivity gives a lower OFL than the model it is derived from, 77.0 kt against 85.6 kt. The run truncated to 2019 is not comparable with the others, since its reference points are computed from a different span of data. [[author: interpret the direction of these changes -- in particular why the corrected bin convention and the additional year of data both lower the $B_{MSY}$ proxy.]]

### Tier 4

The Tier 4 calculation is the basis for the 2026 harvest specification. The SSC assigned this stock to **Tier 4b** when it set the 2025/26 specification (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2), and that subtier is carried here. [[author: confirm 4b still applies on this cycle's status.]] A random-effects model (REMA) is fitted to the observed survey biomass series, the B~MSY~ proxy is taken as the mean of the smoothed series over years before `r .fy(BMSY_WINDOW_END)`, and stock status is the terminal smoothed biomass relative to that proxy. Target fishing mortality is F = M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^, the median of the prior on natural mortality.

Three currencies are carried, as in the September 2025 assessment: morphometrically mature males, large males (>= 95 mm carapace width), and preferred males (> 101 mm). The observed survey biomass for each, in the terminal survey year and the year preceding it, is:

```{r survey-currencies, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
svy_tab <- data.frame(
  Currency = c("Morphometrically mature males", "Large males (>= 95 mm)",
               "Preferred males (> 101 mm)"),
  `2025`   = c(survey_morph_2025, survey_large_2025, survey_pref_2025),
  `2026`   = c(survey_morph_2026, survey_large_2026, survey_pref_2026),
  check.names = FALSE
)
flextable::flextable(svy_tab) |>
  flextable::colformat_double(digits = 2) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = paste("Observed NMFS summer survey male biomass (1,000 t) by currency.",
                    "These are survey observations, not output of any assessment model.",
                    "2025 and 2026. These are the survey observations; the Tier 4",
                    "calculation below is applied to the REMA-smoothed series."),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "survey-currencies")
  )
```

The observed mature male biomass from the `r 2025` survey was `r .f(survey_morph_2025, 2)` kt, against `r .f(survey_morph_2026, 2)` kt in `r 2026`.

Applying the Tier 4 rule to each currency gives:

```{r tier4-currencies, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

names(t4) <- c("Currency", "B_MSY", "B current", "Status", "M", "F_OFL", "OFL",
               "OFL (ramped HCR)", "OFL (Baranov)")[seq_along(t4)]
flextable::flextable(t4) |>
  flextable::colformat_double(digits = 3) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = paste("Tier 4 management quantities by currency (biomass and OFL in",
                    "1,000 t; F per year). Computed from the REMA-smoothed survey",
                    "series, not from a GMACS model.",
                    "F_OFL and OFL are the reported basis: flat F_OFL = M above the",
                    "closure threshold, with OFL = F_OFL x B. The final two columns are",
                    "alternatives, each changing one choice - the ramped control rule,",
                    "and the Baranov catch equation."),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "tier4-currencies")
  )
```

The recommended currency is morphometrically mature male biomass, giving an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026)` kt and, after the `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` buffer, an ABC of `r .f(abc_2026)` kt. [[author: the September 2025 assessment recommended the >= 95 mm currency instead, on the grounds that morphometrically mature male biomass "results in reference points that allow for the complete removal of large males". The choice of currency moves the OFL by more than a factor of four (Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies)) -- far more than either the control-rule or catch-equation choice -- so the reversal needs an explicit justification here.]]

The biomass the control rule acts on carries real uncertainty, and the guidelines require it to be reported. The random-effects fit puts terminal morphometrically mature male biomass at `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt with a 95 percent interval of `r .f(mmb_2026_lci, 2)` to `r .f(mmb_2026_uci, 2)` kt, a coefficient of variation of `r .f(100*mmb_2026_cv, 1)` percent. This is the prediction interval REMA returns for the smoothed series, which reflects the process error the random-effects model estimates. It is not the sampling uncertainty of the survey itself: the survey CVs are an input to the fit, not its output, and the two should not be quoted interchangeably. The interval is lognormal, so the log-scale standard deviation is recovered as (log of the upper bound minus log of the lower bound) divided by 2 x 1.96, and the coefficient of variation follows from it.

Propagating that interval through the control rule, with F~OFL~ flat at M across its whole range, gives an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt with a range of `r .f(ofl_2026_lci, 2)` to `r .f(ofl_2026_uci, 2)` kt, and a stock status of `r .f(status_2026, 3)` with a range of `r .f(status_2026_lci, 3)` to `r .f(status_2026_uci, 3)`. Two features of that status range matter. The lower bound remains above the minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt, so the stock is not overfished at any point in the interval. But the upper bound reaches `r .f(status_2026_uci, 3)`, so on this measure the biomass at which the stock would be considered rebuilt lies inside the interval, even though the point estimate sits below it. The rebuilding determination in Section H should be read with that in mind.

[[author: this interval covers the random-effects smoothing only. It does not include uncertainty in the B~MSY~ proxy, which is the mean of the same smoothed series and is therefore correlated with the terminal estimate, nor uncertainty in the choice of currency or averaging window, both of which move the OFL by more than this interval does. Say so, or widen the treatment.]]

Two alternatives are reported alongside the recommended basis. The first applies the sloped control rule between the closure threshold and B~MSY~ rather than a flat F = M; at the current status this lowers F~OFL~ from `r .f(fofl_2026, 4)` to `r .f(tier4_by_currency$Fofl_ramp[tier4_by_currency$currency == "morphometric"], 4)`. The second computes the OFL from the Baranov catch equation, treating F~OFL~ as an instantaneous rate acting alongside natural mortality over the year, rather than as an annual exploitation fraction. The flat rule is the recommended basis. It follows the groundfish Tier 5 FMP, under which the target rate is the natural mortality rate itself with no ramp, and it follows the Tier 4 calculation presented in the September 2025 assessment, which states explicitly that no kink exists in that harvest control rule. This differs from the basis the SSC used when it set the 2025/26 specification: at a stock status of 0.74 the SSC reported F~OFL~ = 0.19 (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2), where flat F = M would have given 0.27. The sloped rule at that status returns M x (0.74 - 0.10) / (1 - 0.10) = 0.192, and the specified OFL of 20.11 kt divided by the MMB of 105.213 kt implies 0.1911, so the specification was set on the sloped rule. The SSC did use the linear catch equation, as this assessment does; the Baranov form would have returned 16.02 kt rather than 20.11 kt. At this cycle's status of `r .f(status_2026, 3)` the difference between the two rules is an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt against `r .f(ofl_2026_ramp, 2)` kt, and the sloped result is reported above so that the comparison is available. [[author: the divergence from the 2025/26 specification will be asked about. State the argument for the flat rule here in your own terms -- the FMP basis is recorded above, but the reason for departing from the SSC's most recent application is not.]]


## Parameters estimated independently of the assessment

The Tier 4 calculation does not estimate biological parameters. The quantities it takes as given, and their sources, are:

* **Natural mortality**, M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^ for mature males. This is the median of the prior on natural mortality used in the integrated assessment, and it serves as both the target fishing mortality and, under Tiers 4 and 5, the F~limit~.
* **The probability of terminal molt at size**, supplied as a fixed input from the Kodiak laboratory's spatiotemporal `sdmTMB` maturity workflow rather than estimated within the model.
* **Growth per molt and the variance in growth increment**, estimated outside the model from the growth data.
* **Weight at length**, specified from the published relationship.
* **Discard and bycatch mortality rates**, specified rather than estimated.

## F~limit~

Under Tiers 4 and 5 the fishing mortality rate above which the stock is considered to be subject to overfishing is the natural mortality rate itself. For this stock F~limit~ = M = `r .f(NAT_M, 2)` yr^-1^. This is a different quantity from the reverse-engineered F reported for Tier 1--3 stocks, which is the rate that would have produced a catch equal to the previous year's OFL, and that quantity is not computed here.

\newpage

# G. Calculation of the ABC

The recommended acceptable biological catch (ABC) is calculated by subtracting a buffer from the OFL to account for scientific uncertainty. The buffer applied here is `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` percent, giving an ABC of `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt against an OFL of `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt. This buffer accounts for scientific uncertainty not directly captured in the assessment, including retrospective patterns and model misspecification.

[[author: the maximum permissible ABC must be reported regardless of the author's recommendation, with its calculation described (groundfish guidelines 4.11.2; the crab checklist says the same). It is not stated here because the maximum permissible buffer for a Tier 4 crab stock could not be established from the documents to hand --- the June 2026 SSC notes only that the default crab control rule gives a minimal buffer between maxABC and the OFL at P* = 0.49. Supply that basis and report maxABC alongside the recommended ABC.]]  The June 2026 SSC supported reporting a stock-specific history of the buffers applied to the OFL, and suggested that a historical buffer could initially be set at the average buffer from the previous five assessments (Table \@ref(tab:buffer-history)).

```{r buffer-history, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# 2020-2024 as printed in the 2025 SAFE (Section G); 2025 read from Table 2 of
# the October 2025 SSC report. The 2022 value is genuinely not recoverable --
# the October 2022 SSC reports are not posted -- so it is NA rather than a
# guess, and the mean is over the years actually known.
buffer_hist <- data.frame(
  Year   = c(2020L, 2021L, 2022L, 2023L, 2024L, 2025L),
  Buffer = c(25, 25, NA, 50, 65, 40),
  Source = c("2025 SAFE, Section G", "2025 SAFE, Section G",
             "October 2022 SSC reports are not available online",
             "2025 SAFE, Section G", "2025 SAFE, Section G",
             "October 2025 SSC report, Table 2"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
.known <- buffer_hist$Buffer[!is.na(buffer_hist$Buffer)]
buffer_hist$Buffer <- ifelse(is.na(buffer_hist$Buffer), "NA",
                             sprintf("%.0f%%", buffer_hist$Buffer))
names(buffer_hist)[2] <- "SSC buffer (% of OFL)"

flextable::flextable(buffer_hist) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = sprintf(paste("History of the ABC buffer applied by the SSC, as a percentage of the",
                            "OFL. The mean over the %d recoverable years is %.0f%%. The 2022 value",
                            "could not be sourced, so this is the average of five assessments but",
                            "not of the five most recent ones."),
                      length(.known), mean(.known)),
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "buffer-history")
  )
```

The `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1-ABC_buffer))` percent buffer recommended here is the figure the September 2025 assessment also recommended, and is the buffer historically applied to crab stocks whose data and model complexity are sufficient for Tier 3. It is lower than the buffer the SSC has applied to this stock in recent years. For the 2025/26 specification the SSC applied a 40 percent buffer, setting an ABC of 12.07 kt against an OFL of 20.11 kt (October 2025 SSC report, Table 2), and against the recoverable history in Table \@ref(tab:buffer-history) a 20 percent buffer would be the smallest applied to this stock in any of the six years shown and less than half the 41 percent average over the five recoverable years. Three of the four risk table categories score Level 1, Normal (Table \@ref(tab:risk-table)). [[author: the reduction from 40 percent to 20 percent is the single largest departure in this document from the last specification, and it moves the ABC in the same direction as the control-rule choice rather than offsetting it. Compounded, the two put the recommended ABC at `r .f(abc_2026, 2)` kt where the basis the SSC used for 2025/26 -- sloped rule, 40 percent buffer -- would give `r .f(0.6*ofl_2026_ramp, 2)` kt on this cycle's biomass, a factor of `r .f(abc_2026/(0.6*ofl_2026_ramp), 2)`. That is the number the CPT will arrive at, so the document should reach it first. It needs your argument, and the assessment-related risk category -- still unscored -- is where the supporting evidence for it belongs. The June 2026 SSC cautioned against a predetermined direction in modifying any buffer.]]

## Risk table

The risk table follows the four categories used for groundfish, in the tiered form the June 2026 SSC described: a long-term row capturing persistent uncertainty, which is what justifies a base or historical buffer, and a current-year row for year-specific risk. The SSC scopes the long-term row to the assessment and population-dynamics categories only, which is why the ecosystem and fishery cells in that row are not scored.

The population-dynamics, ecosystem and fishery-informed cells below are taken from the 2026 risk table summary prepared from the ESP (Fedewa and Shotwell 2026), the AFSC Spring Preview of Ecosystem and Economic Conditions Workshop, and the eastern Bering Sea Ecosystem Status Report (Siddon 2026, in press). The ESP is Appendix A to this assessment.

```{r risk-table, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}

  Category = c("Assessment-related", "Population dynamics",

    paste("[[author: assign a level. The evidence: multimodality has persisted across cycles and is",

## Status determination

**Is the stock subject to overfishing?** No. Overfishing is determined by comparing the catch from the most recent complete crab year with the OFL specified for that year. Total catch in 2025/26 was 7.10 kt --- 4.13 kt retained, 2.52 kt of male discards, 0.03 kt of female discards and 0.42 kt of trawl bycatch --- against the OFL of 20.11 kt that the SSC specified for 2025/26 in October 2025. Catch was 35 percent of the specified OFL.

**Is the stock overfished?** The stock was determined to be overfished for 2024/25, with mature male biomass of 60.08 kt against a minimum stock size threshold of 71.40 kt (October 2025 SSC report, Table 1), and it remains in the rebuilding plan adopted under Amendment 53. On this cycle's estimate mature male biomass is `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt against a minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt, so the stock is above the threshold on the current estimate and across the whole of its 95 percent interval (Section F).

**Is the stock approaching an overfished condition?** [[author: this determination is required of the author and is not made here. Note that the groundfish guidelines scope both the overfished and the approaching-overfished statements to Tiers 1--3; the crab checklist does not, and the stock is in a rebuilding plan, so both are stated.]]

[[author: the catch convention needs one check. The figure above is observed catch. The SSC's Table 1 reports total catch of 2.81 kt for 2024/25 where the same summation on the assessment's own inputs gives 2.90 kt, so the SSC applies a handling-mortality weighting this does not. The determination is unaffected --- catch is far below the OFL on either convention --- but match the convention before the table is published.]]

## Author recommendations

The June 2026 SSC recommended that only the Tier 4 model be brought forward in October, to allow time for the development of a simpler and more stable Tier 3 model. The overfishing limit in this document is calculated on that basis. The Tier 3 models are presented to document progress and are not proposed for specification.

Three questions the May 2026 preliminary assessment put to the CPT and SSC have since been settled and are not reopened here. The composition correction and the expanded plus group were endorsed as technical corrections and are carried in every September model. The immature survey index was rejected as a convergence fix, on the grounds that it shifts the model toward higher natural mortality among mature males and raises a question of duplicative use of the same survey data. Hybrid catch data were judged premature for inclusion in the snow and Tanner crab assessment models, with hybrid-related uncertainty to be handled instead through the risk table, the ABC buffer, or the TAC-setting process.

[[author: state the recommended Tier 4 configuration -- currency, control rule, and buffer -- and the reasoning. Three decisions are open and each moves the OFL materially: (a) the currency. Morphometric maturity gives `r .f(ofl_2026, 2)` kt against `r .f(tier4_by_currency$OFL[tier4_by_currency$currency == ">95 mm"], 2)` kt on >= 95 mm and `r .f(tier4_by_currency$OFL[tier4_by_currency$currency == ">101 mm"], 2)` kt on > 101 mm (Table \@ref(tab:tier4-currencies)). The 2025 assessment recommended >= 95 mm, arguing that morphometric reference points permit the removal of essentially all large males while the trend in large males is firmly negative. That argument has not been answered here; (b) the control rule. This document applies a flat F = M above the closure threshold, which follows the 2025 Tier 4 calculation and the groundfish Tier 5 FMP. At a status of `r .f(status_2026, 3)` the stock is below B~MSY~ and under a rebuilding plan, where the crab FMP subtier would ordinarily ramp; the sloped alternative is reported alongside; (c) the buffer. See the ABC section.]]

[[author: the September 2026 meeting notes call for a discussion of author priorities against SSC priorities and where they diverge. The SSC's stated priority is a simplified Tier 3 model -- fixing the recruitment sex ratio at 50:50, reducing confounding among growth, natural mortality and selectivity, estimating growth externally, and considering an earlier equilibrium start year -- in preference to further iterations of the current base model. The male-only model (`Model 26.1`) is a first step in that direction and is reported here. State where the author's priorities differ and why.]]

# H. Rebuilding analysis and update

[[author: this section is required both by the SAFE guidelines and by the rebuilding plan itself -- Amendment 53 states that the BSAI Crab Plan Team would report stock status and progress towards the rebuilt level in this document. The September 2025 assessment did not include it, which the SSC noted in October 2025. Placed here un-lettered pending the section-lettering decision; the guidelines number it H.]]

## Status of the rebuilding plan

On 19 October 2021 NMFS determined, and notified the Council, that the eastern Bering Sea snow crab stock was overfished, the estimated mature male biomass having fallen below the minimum stock size threshold specified in the fishery management plan. The Council developed a rebuilding plan under section 304(e) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, adopted as **Amendment 53** to the Fishery Management Plan for Bering Sea/Aleutian Islands King and Tanner Crabs and implemented before the start of the 2023/24 fishing season.

The rebuilding analysis set the minimum time to rebuild in the absence of fishing (T~min~) at 6 years, which under the National Standard 1 guidelines sets a maximum time to rebuild (T~max~) of 10 years. **The stock is considered rebuilt when mature male biomass reaches B~MSY~.** Median projections placed rebuilding in 2029 under no fishing, under bycatch only, and under the State harvest strategy, and in 2030 under fishing at the ABC, The 5th inter-simulation percentile is 2027 across all scenarios. The 95th is 2034 under no fishing and under bycatch only; under the State harvest strategy and under fishing at the ABC the upper tail does not rebuild within the projection horizon. If mortality events of the kind observed in 2018--19 recur in roughly one year in seven, the projected rebuilding time extends to 2034. The analysis concluded that the main driver of the rate of rebuilding is recruitment and the ecosystem conditions that permit it, rather than fishing mortality.

## Relationship to previous rebuilding plans

This is the third rebuilding plan for the stock. Snow crab was first declared overfished on 24 September 1999, and a rebuilding plan was adopted as Amendment 14 in 2000. The Amendment 53 environmental assessment's reference list cites Amendment 15 for that plan, but the 2000 environmental assessment itself is titled for Amendment 14 (NPFMC, ADF&G and NMFS staff, December 2000), and Amendment 14 is the citation carried here. In 2009 the NMFS Alaska Region notified the Council that the stock would not be rebuilt by the end of that rebuilding period, 2009/10, and that a revised plan was required; Amendment 39 followed. Amendment 53 replaces those earlier provisions, which were removed from the fishery management plan when it was adopted.

## Progress toward rebuilding

[[author: state progress on the basis actually adopted for the specification. The quantities below are from the Tier 4 calculation on the recommended currency and will need to be restated if the currency or the control rule changes.]]

Mature male biomass is estimated at `r .f(mmb_2026, 2)` kt against a B~MSY~ proxy of `r .f(bmsy_2026, 2)` kt, or `r .f(100*status_2026, 0)` percent of the proxy, with a minimum stock size threshold of `r .f(msst_2026, 2)` kt. The stock is therefore above its minimum stock size threshold but has not, on the point estimate, reached the biomass at which it would be considered rebuilt. Accounting for the uncertainty in the random-effects fit (Section F), status is `r .f(status_2026, 3)` with a 95 percent range of `r .f(status_2026_lci, 3)` to `r .f(status_2026_uci, 3)`. The lower end remains above the threshold for an overfished determination; the upper end reaches the rebuilt threshold. On this basis the stock cannot be declared rebuilt, but neither can rebuilding be excluded on the terminal-year estimate alone.

## Recruitment

Because the rebuilding analysis identifies recruitment as the main driver of the rebuilding rate, recruitment is reported here directly. Estimated male recruitment collapsed to 0.088 and 0.065 billion crab in 2018 and 2019, among the lowest in the time series, before rising to 1.65, 2.36 and 4.28 billion in 2020, 2021 and 2022 and settling near 1.0 billion in 2024 and 2025. The mean over the last five years, 2.01 billion, is above the 1982--2019 mean of 1.22 billion.

That comparison should be treated with caution. Terminal-year recruitment is the least well determined quantity in the assessment: the retrospective analysis gives a Mohn's rho for male recruitment of `r .fmt(.rho("standard","recruitment_male"), 2)`, meaning that recent recruitment estimates revise substantially as data accumulate. The apparent post-collapse recruitment pulse is consistent with the survey observing small crab, but its magnitude in the terminal years should not be relied on. [[author: compare against the survey-derived recruit index produced by `04_plot_recruitment_comparison.R` (`plots/recruitment_survey_vs_model.png`), which is not yet included as a numbered figure; the correlation between the model's estimated recruitment and the survey recruit index over the overlapping period is negative, which deserves comment.]]

\newpage

# I. Data gaps and research priorities

Several data and structural issues identified warrant follow-up:

* **Hybrid identification consistency between ADF&G and NMFS.** ADF&G classifies hybrid crab into three categories (opilio-type, bairdi-type, and unspecified) using a hybrid identification key based on eye color, epistome shape, and secondary morphological characteristics. ADF&G and NMFS do not currently agree on the number of secondary characteristics required for a positive hybrid identification, and the unspecified-hybrid category are present in a non-trivial portion of the time series. Resolving identification criteria across agencies and propagating the resulting categorization back through the historical observer time series would improve the hybrid-data products available to the assessment. However, the value add to the snow crab assessment may be minimal given the low percentage of opilio-type hybrids in the data.

* **Apportionment of retained catch between snow crab and hybrids.** Hybrids are currently retained under either the snow-crab or the Tanner-crab IFQ depending on regulatory identification but are not separately tracked in the retained-catch data. ADF&G has indicated it does not yet have a method for partitioning historical retained catch into hybrid versus parent species. Developing such a partitioning would allow the hybrid sensitivity to be explored more fully (presently the retained time-series is identical between the hybrid and non-hybrid models because retained catch already contains hybrids).

* **Quality control on early hybrid catch estimates.** The ADF&G hybrid total-catch estimates contain unexpectedly large values in 1997 (~18 kt of legal-male hybrid catch) and 1998 (~15 kt), with high-CPUE pots peppered around the fishery footprint rather than concentrated in obvious hot spots. ADF&G has flagged these years as requiring follow-up before the data should be considered reliable for regular assessment use.

* **Maturity workflow comparison.** The new spatiotemporal maturity workflow produces a much weaker temporal trend in the probability of terminal molt at size than the legacy workflow. Side-by-side documentation of the two workflows, an evaluation of the spatial sample sizes of chela measurements (which are sparse at many stations and many sizes), uncertainty, and quantification of the degrees of freedom consumed by the spatial process would help the CPT and SSC evaluate the two approaches.

* **Source of bimodality in the snow crab assessment.** Although the immature survey index appears to remove the bimodal jitter signal in the May 2026 candidate models, the underlying source of multiple optima is not understood. A focused investigation of which parameter combinations produce the two clouds (e.g., recruitment in the most recent years, $M$ events, or selectivity parameters) would help clarify whether the immature index is solving a real problem or is masking it.

* **Reproductive biology of large male snow crab.** As noted in 2024 and 2025 SSC comments, more research is needed on whether small males can and do mate with large females and produce progeny that will be large males under favorable environmental conditions. This question remains the main axis of uncertainty because the fishery cannot exist without large males and large males are at historical lows.

# J. Ecosystem considerations

See the ESP for snow crab specific indices of environmental variation that may be relevant to stock dynamics (Appendix A). See the risk table (Table \@ref(tab:risk-table)) for factors that may influence the choice of buffer. [[author: the crab checklist lists the buffer history and the risk table as an appendix; both currently sit in Section G, where the ABC reasoning uses them. Move them if the appendix placement is preferred.]] More broadly, scientific frameworks that quantify tradeoffs among fisheries would be useful in decision making and scientific communication.

# Auxiliary files

The following files accompany this assessment and are archived with it. All are in the native format of the assessment program.

* `26_snow_update_newmat_plus_group.dat` --- the model data file.
* `snow.ctl` --- the control file, naming the estimated parameters, their bounds and phases.
* `snow.prj` --- the projection file.
* `gmacs.dat` and `gmacs_files_in.dat` --- the run configuration and the file manifest GMACS reads.
* `gmacs.pin` --- the starting parameter vector. For the accepted fit this is the jitter winner's parameter vector rather than a cold start; its provenance is recorded in `jitter/PROMOTION.md`.
* `gmacs` --- the model executable (GMACS 2.20.34, macOS arm64). `gmacs.exe` is the corresponding Windows build.
* The six derived input files that form the interface between the data preparation scripts and the model: `directed_catch.csv`, `bycatch_catch.csv`, `fishery_size_comps.csv`, `survey_size_comps.csv`, `survey_indices.csv` and `male_maturity_ogive.csv`.

**Appendix A. Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile.** The ESP is provided as a separate document: Fedewa, E. and Shotwell, K. 2026. *Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile of the eastern Bering Sea snow crab stock --- Update.* It is the source of the ecosystem and fishery-informed indicators summarised in the risk table (Table \@ref(tab:risk-table)) and of the indicator series referenced in Section J.

**Appendix B. Removals from sources other than commercial catch.** [[author: an appendix of non-commercial removals is required (groundfish guidelines 4.23; the internal review checklist asks for an appendix table of removals from sources other than official catch estimates). No such data exists anywhere in this repository --- `data/adfg_removals/` holds directed retained catch, directed discards, trawl bycatch and other-crab bycatch, all of which are commercial removals already carried in the model, and the September 2025 assessment does not report non-commercial removals either. Survey removals, and any research, subsistence or personal-use take, would need to be obtained before this table can be built. State the amounts, or state that they are negligible and on what basis.]]

```{r like-index-tot, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}

extract_likelihoods <- function(path) {
  out_file <- file.path(path, "Gmacsall.out")
  if (!file.exists(out_file)) return(NULL)

  tmp <- readLines(out_file)

  # Pull the Raw_likelihood vector for a labeled sub-block of
  # Likelihoods_by_type_and_fleet (e.g. "Catches", "Index", "Size_composition").
  get_raw <- function(label) {
    hdr <- grep(paste0("^--", label, ": list"), tmp)[1]
    if (is.na(hdr)) return(numeric(0))
    eol_offset <- grep("^>EOL<", tmp[(hdr + 1):length(tmp)])[1]
    block <- tmp[(hdr + 1):(hdr + eol_offset - 1)]
    raw <- block[grep("^Raw_likelihood", block)][1]
    parts <- strsplit(trimws(sub("^Raw_likelihood\\s*:?\\s*", "", raw)), "\\s+")[[1]]
    as.numeric(parts)
  }

  catch_lbls <- c("Catch: Pot retained M", "Catch: Pot discarded M",
                  "Catch: Pot discarded F", "Catch: Trawl bycatch")
  index_lbls <- c("Index: NMFS 1982 F mature", "Index: NMFS 1989 F mature",
                  "Index: NMFS 1982 M mature", "Index: NMFS 1989 M mature")
  size_lbls  <- c("Size: Pot M retained", "Size: Pot M total", "Size: Pot F discarded",
                  "Size: Trawl F discarded", "Size: Trawl M discarded",
                  "Size: NMFS 1982 F immature", "Size: NMFS 1989 F immature",
                  "Size: NMFS 1982 M immature", "Size: NMFS 1989 M immature",
                  "Size: NMFS 1982 F mature",   "Size: NMFS 1989 F mature",
                  "Size: NMFS 1982 M mature",   "Size: NMFS 1989 M mature")

  pad <- function(x, n) { length(x) <- n; x }
  catch_vals <- pad(get_raw("Catches"),          length(catch_lbls))
  index_vals <- pad(get_raw("Index"),            length(index_lbls))
  size_vals  <- pad(get_raw("Size_composition"), length(size_lbls))

  # Other components (SRR, Tag, Growth, Penalties, Priors, ...) still come from
  # the aggregate Likelihoods_by_type block.
  st  <- grep("^Likelihoods_by_type: list", tmp)[1]
  eol_offset <- grep("^>EOL<", tmp[(st + 1):length(tmp)])[1]
  rows <- tmp[(st + 1):(st + eol_offset - 1)]
  clean_rows <- gsub(":", "", rows)
  parts <- strsplit(trimws(clean_rows), " +")
  vals <- sapply(parts, function(x) as.numeric(tail(x, 1)))
  names(vals) <- sapply(parts, function(x) x[1])

  other_keys <- c("Stock_recruitment", "Tagging_data", "Growth_data",
                  "Penalties", "Priors", "Positive_growth_penalty",
                  "Total", "Initial_size_structure")
  other_lbls <- c("SRR", "Tag", "Growth", "Penalties", "Priors",
                  "Positive_growth_penalty", "Total", "Initial_size_structure")
  other_vals <- unname(vals[other_keys])

  dat <- data.frame(
    Object = c(catch_lbls, index_lbls, size_lbls, other_lbls),
    Value  = c(catch_vals, index_vals, size_vals, other_vals)
  )
  colnames(dat)[2] <- path
  return(dat)
}

# models_present: a folder that does not exist yields a column of zeros here
# (see tot_likes[is.na(...)] <- 0 below), which reads as "all likelihood
# components are zero" rather than "this model was not run".
tot_likes <- lapply(models_present, extract_likelihoods)

# extract_likelihoods() returns NULL when a model directory has no Gmacsall.out
# -- a fit that never finished writing, not a missing folder, so the dir.exists()
# guard above does not catch it. Left to purrr::reduce() that surfaces as
# `auto_copy(): x and y must share the same src ... y is NULL`, which names
# neither the chunk's real problem nor the model. Name it instead. Hit
# 2026-08-28: Model 25.2e had a complete fit but no Gmacsall.out, and it killed
# the whole render at chunk 18 of 93.
.bad <- names(models_present)[vapply(tot_likes, is.null, logical(1))]
if (length(.bad))
  stop("No Gmacsall.out for: ", paste(to_short(.bad), collapse = ", "),
       ". Re-fit the model, or run gmacs -binp gmacs.bar -hess_step 5 in its ",
       "directory to regenerate the outputs from the existing MLE.")

tot_likes <- tot_likes %>% purrr::reduce(dplyr::full_join)

tot_likes[is.na(tot_likes)] <- 0
rownames(tot_likes) <- tot_likes$Object
tot_likes <- tot_likes[,-1]
colnames(tot_likes) <- as.character(to_short(names(models_present)))

# Render with flextable so the caption produces a Word bookmark/sequence
# field that bookdown's \@ref(tab:like-comp-tot) can resolve. Transposed so
# that models are rows and likelihood components are columns to better fit
# the landscape page.
tot_likes_t <- as.data.frame(t(signif(tot_likes, 5)), check.names = FALSE)
tot_likes_df <- data.frame(
  Model       = rownames(tot_likes_t),
  tot_likes_t,
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Diagnostic dump of the likelihood components, one file per knit date. Nothing
# reads it back -- it exists so the components can be diffed between renders.
# Written to data/diagnostics/, not the repo root: the root is off limits, and
# data/derived/ is the six-file model interface, which this is not part of.
dir.create("data/diagnostics", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
write.csv(tot_likes_t,
          file = file.path("data/diagnostics",
                           paste0("likelihood_components_", Sys.Date(), ".csv")))

index_and_catch <- tot_likes_t %>%
  select(contains("Catch") | contains("Index")) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), round, 2))
index_and_catch <- cbind(data.frame(Model = rownames(tot_likes_t)), index_and_catch)

flextable::flextable(index_and_catch) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Catch and index likelihood components (negative log-likelihood, dimensionless) by fleet and model.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "like-index-tot")
  )

```{r max-grad, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}

extract_max_gradient <- function(path) {
  grad_file <- file.path(path, "gradient.dat")
  if (!file.exists(grad_file)) {
    return(data.frame(NPar = NA_integer_, Parameter = NA_character_, MaxAbsGradient = NA_real_))
  }
  grad <- read.table(grad_file, header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  idx <- which.max(abs(grad$Gradient))
  data.frame(
    NPar           = nrow(grad),
    Parameter      = grad$ParName[idx],
    MaxAbsGradient = abs(grad$Gradient[idx])
  )
}

# models_present, not model_defs: extract_max_gradient() returns an all-NA row
# for a folder that does not exist, which would render as a blank row here.
gradlist <- list()
for(i in seq_along(models_present)){

  out <- extract_max_gradient(models_present[i])
 gradlist[[i]] <- data.frame(
    Model          = to_short(names(models_present)[i]),
    NPar           = out$NPar,
    Parameter      = out$Parameter,
    MaxAbsGradient = round(out$MaxAbsGradient, 5)
  )
}
max_grad_df <- do.call("rbind", gradlist)

colnames(max_grad_df) <- c("Model", "N parameters", "Parameter", "Max |gradient|")

flextable::flextable(max_grad_df) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Maximum absolute value gradient (dimensionless) and corresponding parameter for each candidate model.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "max-grad")
  )

```

```{r retro-rho, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}

# Mohn's rho, written by 06_run_retrospective.R (retro_rho loaded in retro-setup).
if (is.null(retro_rho)) {
  cat("*Retrospective results not yet generated; run `06_run_retrospective.R`.*")
} else {
  rho_tab <- data.frame(
    Quantity = c(mature_male_biomass = "Mature male biomass",
                 recruitment_male    = "Male recruitment")[retro_rho$quantity],
    Retrospective = c(standard    = "Standard",
                      drop_survey = "Terminal survey dropped")[retro_rho$mode],
    Peels          = retro_rho$n_peels,
    MohnsRho       = round(retro_rho$mohns_rho, 3),
    RalstonsSigma  = round(retro_rho$ralstons_sigma, 3),
    MinRel         = round(retro_rho$min_rel_diff, 3),
    MaxRel         = round(retro_rho$max_rel_diff, 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL
  )
  colnames(rho_tab) <- c("Quantity", "Retrospective", "Peels", "Mohn's rho",
                         "Ralston's sigma", "Min rel. diff.", "Max rel. diff.")

  flextable::flextable(rho_tab) |>
    flextable::autofit() |>
    flextable::set_caption(
      caption = paste("Retrospective statistics by configuration and model.",
                      "Mohn's rho and Ralston's sigma are dimensionless.",
                      "Mohn's rho is the mean over peels of",
                      "(peel - full model) / full model at each peel's terminal year, so a",
                      "positive value means terminal estimates are revised downward as data",
                      "accumulate. Ralston's sigma is the log-scale RMSE of the same",
                      "terminal-year pairs. The dropped-terminal-survey peels are compared",
                      "against the full model fit to all data."),
      autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "retro-rho")
    )
}

        ),

```{r stepchange, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F}
# Define the target management parameters to extract
# We map the GMACS label to the column index based on your logic:
# BMSY, Status, FMSY usually in index 3; FOFL, OFL in index 4.
mgmt_targets <- list(
  "BMSY"   = 3,
  "Bcurr/BMSY" = 3,
  "Fmsy"   = 4,
  "Fofl"   = 4,
  "OFL"    = 3
)

# Helper function to extract management quantities from one model folder
extract_mgmt_quantities <- function(path, model_name) {
  out_file <- file.path(path, "Gmacsall.out")
  if (!file.exists(out_file)) return(NULL)

  tmp <- readLines(out_file)

  # Identify the summary block
  st  <- grep("BMSY", tmp)[1]
  end <- grep("Ofl", tmp) |> tail(1)
  mgmt_block <- tmp[st:end]

  # Extract values based on targets
  values <- lapply(names(mgmt_targets), function(target) {
    line <- mgmt_block[grep(target, mgmt_block)][1]
    if (is.na(line)) return(NA)

    # Split by one or more spaces
    parts <- unlist(strsplit(trimws(line), " "))
    idx   <- mgmt_targets[[target]]
    return(as.numeric(parts[idx]))
  })

  names(values) <- names(mgmt_targets)

  # Extract male natural mortality (immature and mature) for the most recent
  # year. M is constant across the 22 size classes, so the first size-class
  # column is sufficient.
  m_start <- grep("Natural_mortality-by-class: dataframe", tmp, fixed = TRUE)[1]
  m_imm <- NA_real_
  m_mat <- NA_real_
  if (!is.na(m_start)) {
    eod_rel <- grep(">EOD<", tmp[(m_start + 1):length(tmp)], fixed = TRUE)[1]
    m_end <- m_start + eod_rel - 1
    m_block <- tmp[(m_start + 2):(m_end - 1)]
    m_df <- utils::read.table(text = m_block, header = FALSE,
                              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    colnames(m_df)[1:4] <- c("Year", "Sex", "Maturity", "M")
    males <- m_df[m_df$Sex == "male", ]
    latest <- max(males$Year, na.rm = TRUE)
    m_imm <- males$M[males$Year == latest & males$Maturity == "immature"][1]
    m_mat <- males$M[males$Year == latest & males$Maturity == "mature"][1]
  }
  values[["M (imm males)"]] <- as.numeric(m_imm)
  values[["M (mat males)"]] <- as.numeric(m_mat)

  return(dplyr::as_tibble(values) |> dplyr::mutate(Model = model_name))
}

# Iterate over the models this cycle ran, not the retained May bracket -- this is
# the table the OFL/BMSY comparison is read from, so a row per non-existent model
# would put NA management quantities in front of the CPT.
ref_table <- names(models_present) |>
  purrr::map_dfr(~extract_mgmt_quantities(models_present[.x], .x)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Model = to_short(Model)) |>
  dplyr::select(Model, everything()) # Reorder to put Model first

# Render with flextable so \@ref(tab:stepchange) resolves in Word output.
flextable::flextable(ref_table) |>
  flextable::colformat_double(digits = 2) |>
  flextable::autofit() |>
  flextable::set_caption(
    caption = "Management quantities by model, derived from maximum likelihood estimates using Tier 3 reference points. Biomass and OFL in 1,000 t; fishing and natural mortality rates in per year. Reported natural mortality is for immature and mature males in the terminal year of the assessment, average recruitment is for males, and status and MMB were estimates for February 15 of the completed crab year.",
    autonum = officer::run_autonum(seq_id = "tab", pre_label = "Table ", bkm = "stepchange")
  )
```

# --- 1. Extract Weight and Results ---
# Direct indexing instead of eval(parse)
rep_obj     <- reslst$repsLst[[names(report_model)]]
weight_data <- rep_obj$IndivWeightByXM

# Extract weight-at-length vectors (assuming 22 size classes)
male_wt   <- weight_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(Sex == "male", Year == 1982, Maturity == 'mature') |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^[0-9]")) |> as.numeric()

female_wt <- weight_data |> 
  dplyr::filter(Sex == "female", Year == 1982, Maturity == 'mature') |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^[0-9]")) |> as.numeric()

# --- 2. Extract Population Numbers (N) ---
# Helper to extract dataframe sections from Gmacsall.out without manual loops
extract_gmacs_df <- function(lines, header) {
  start <- grep(header, lines, fixed = TRUE) + 1
  end   <- grep("EOD", lines[start:length(lines)])[1] + start - 2
  read.table(text = lines[start:end])
}

gmacs_lines <- readLines(file.path(report_model, "/Gmacsall.out"))
n_males_mat <- extract_gmacs_df(gmacs_lines, "N(males_mature): dataframe")
n_females_mat <- extract_gmacs_df(gmacs_lines, "N(females_mature): dataframe")

# --- 3. Extract Selectivity ---
dfrSel <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "selfcns") |> 
  dplyr::filter(type == "capture", fleet == "NMFS_Trawl_1989", 
                case == names(report_model), sex == 'male', year == 2023)

# Ensure selectivity vector length matches size classes (22)
male_sel <- dfrSel |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^[0-9]")) |> as.numeric()

# --- 4. Define Size Filters ---
# Logic for biomass/abundance tiers based on carapace width (CW)
sizes <- seq(27.5, 132.5, 5)
mask_95  <- ifelse(sizes >= 95, 1.0, 0.0)

# User-specific logic for >105mm: 
# Includes 50% of the 97.5 bin
# Standardizing to the logic in your snippet:
mask_101 <- dplyr::case_when(
  sizes > 105  ~ 1.0,
  sizes == 102.5 ~ 0.5, 
  TRUE         ~ 0.0
)


midpoints <- seq(27.5, 132.5, by = 5)

# --- 5. Vectorized Calculations ---
# Convert N dataframes to matrices (excluding Year column)
mat_males   <- as.matrix(n_males_mat[-1, -1])
mat_females <- as.matrix(n_females_mat[-1, -1])

# Calculate Biomass and Abundance (in 1,000 t or billions)
results_tab <- data.frame(
  Year = n_males_mat[-1, 1],
  MMB_95   = (mat_males %*% (male_wt * male_sel * mask_95)) / 1e6,
  MMB_101  = (mat_males %*% (male_wt * male_sel * mask_101)) / 1e6,
  Abund_101 = (mat_males %*% (male_sel * mask_101)) / 1e3,
  # Population (True Values)
  FMB_tot      = (mat_females %*% female_wt) / 1e6,
  MMB_tot      = (mat_males %*% male_wt) / 1e6,
  MMB_95_tot   = (mat_males %*% (male_wt * mask_95)) / 1e6,
  MMB_101_tot  = (mat_males %*% (male_wt * mask_101)) / 1e6,
  Abund_101_tot = (mat_males %*% mask_101) / 1e3
)

survey_results <- data.frame(
  # Predicted (Subject to Survey Selectivity)
  Year      = wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |> 
    filter(sex == 'female', case == names(report_model)) |> pull(year),
  FMB      = wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |> 
    filter(sex == 'female', case == names(report_model)) |> pull(prd),
  MMB      = wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |> 
    filter(sex == 'male', case == names(report_model)) |> pull(prd)
)

# --- 6. Final Table Formatting ---
PlotTab <- survey_results |> 
  full_join(results_tab) |> 
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) |>
  mutate(across(-Year, ~round(.x, 2))) %>%
  select(Year, FMB, MMB, MMB_95, MMB_101, Abund_101, FMB_tot, MMB_tot, MMB_95_tot, MMB_101_tot, Abund_101_tot) %>%
  arrange(Year)

pander::pander(
  PlotTab,
  split.cells = 10,
  split.table = Inf,
  caption = "\\label{predsurvbio}Maximum likelihood estimates of mature male (MMB) and female (FMB) biomass. Columns 2-6 are subject to survey selectivity; columns 7-11 are population values."
)

```{r predtotnum, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval = FALSE}
# --- 0. Helper + load Gmacsall.out ---
# Inlined here so this chunk does not depend on the eval=FALSE chunk above.
extract_gmacs_df <- function(lines, header) {
  start <- grep(header, lines, fixed = TRUE) + 1
  end   <- grep("EOD", lines[start:length(lines)])[1] + start - 2
  read.table(text = lines[start:end])
}

gmacs_lines <- readLines(file.path(report_model, "/Gmacsall.out"))

# --- 1. Extract Data Using Helper ---
n_males   <- extract_gmacs_df(gmacs_lines, "N(males): dataframe")
n_females <- extract_gmacs_df(gmacs_lines, "N(females): dataframe")

# --- 2. Vectorized Calculation ---
# Convert to matrices and drop the first two metadata columns (Year, Season)
mat_m <- as.matrix(n_males[-1, -1])
mat_f <- as.matrix(n_females[-1, -1])

# Calculate row sums for both matrices and convert to billions
# (Assumes model units are in thousands)
total_n_billions <- (rowSums(mat_m) + rowSums(mat_f)) / 1e6

# --- 3. Final Table Assembly ---
tmp_mat <- data.frame(
  `Survey year`   = n_males[-1, 1],
  `Total numbers` = round(total_n_billions, 2),
  check.names     = FALSE
)

# --- 4. Render Table (kable for bookdown table cross-references in Word) ---
knitr::kable(
  tmp_mat,
  caption = "(\\#tab:predtotnum) Maximum likelihood estimates of total numbers of crab (billions), not subject to survey selectivity at the time of the survey."
)

```{r,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=F, eval = FALSE}

# --- 1. Extract Summary Data for all targeted cases ---
# extractRep1Results returns a tidy dataframe containing 'case'
summary_all <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Summary") |> 
  dplyr::filter(case %in% case_for_data_table) |> 
  dplyr::select(case, year, SSB, rec_male) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.numeric(year))

# --- 2. Extract Fishing Mortality for all targeted cases ---
# We loop through the case vector to pull the internal list objects
fm_all <- case_for_data_table |> 
  purrr::map_dfr(function(c_name) {
    rep_obj <- reslst$repsLst[[c_name]]
    
    # Identify the correct dataframe name for this specific model
    # Checks for "capture_rate" first, then "FM"
    f_df_name <- intersect(names(rep_obj), 
                           c("Fully-selected_capture_rate_by_season_sex_and_fishery", 
                             "Fully-selected_FM_by_season_sex_and_fishery"))[1]
    
    if (is.na(f_df_name)) {
      message("Warning: No F-mortality data found for case: ", c_name)
      return(NULL)
    }
    
    rep_obj[[f_df_name]] |> 
      dplyr::filter(sex == 'male', fleet == "Pot_Fishery") |> 
      dplyr::transmute(
        case = c_name,
        year = as.numeric(year),
        f_mort = as.numeric(`2`) # Directed fishing season
      )
  })

# --- 3. Join and Format for Comparison ---
# Use a join to ensure the FM and MMB align correctly for every model
sum_mat <- summary_all |>
  dplyr::inner_join(fm_all, by = c("case", "year")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Model                 = as.character(to_short(case)),
    `Survey Year`         = year,
    `Mature Male Biomass` = round(as.numeric(SSB), 2),
    `Male Recruits`       = round(as.numeric(rec_male) / 1e6, 2), # Billions
    `Fishing Mortality`   = round(f_mort, 2)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Model, `Survey Year`)

# --- 4. Render Table ---
pander::pander(
  sum_mat,
  split.cells = 10,
  caption = "\\label{predsurvbio_tot} Comparison of mature male biomass (MMB) at mating, male recruitment (billions), and fully-selected fishing mortality ($F$) across selected models."
)

```{r surveyplots, echo=FALSE, eval=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, width = 12, height = 7, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Observed male survey biomass for models across hybrid and maturity workflow scenarios."}
dfrIndxFit_plot <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary")  %>%
  dplyr::filter(case %in% c("25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + imm_surv)", # base
                            "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + hyb_surv)", # base + hybrid
                            "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + new_mat + imm_surv)", # base with newmat
                            "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + hyb_both + new_mat)") & # base + hybrid + newmat
             sex == "male" )   %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Categorize index
    Index_category = case_when(
      case == "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + imm_surv)" ~ "Base",
      case ==  "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + hyb_surv)" ~ "Base + hybrid",
      case ==  "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + new_mat + imm_surv)" ~ "Base + newmat",
      case ==  "25.1 gmacs (update + compfix + plus group + hyb_both + new_mat)" ~ "Base + hybrid + newmat",
      .default = NA
    )) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    
    # Confidence interval calculations
    sd_log = sqrt(log(1 + as.numeric(actual_CV)^2)),
    obs = as.numeric(obs),
    lba    = qlnorm(0.05, log(obs), sd_log),
    uba    = qlnorm(0.95, log(obs), sd_log),
    year = as.numeric(year)
  )

# --- Generate the 4-Panel Plot ---
p_idx_final <- ggplot() +
  # Observations (Single black error bar per year/sex/panel)
  geom_errorbar(
    data = dfrIndxFit_plot,
    aes(x = year, ymin = lba, ymax = uba, color = Index_category), 
    width = 0.3, 
    position = position_dodge(width=0.5),
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  # Observations (Single black point per year/sex/panel)
  geom_point(
    data = dfrIndxFit_plot,
    position = position_dodge(width=0.5),
    aes(x = year, y = obs, color = Index_category), 
    size = 1.2
  ) +
  # Formatting and Scales
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    x = "Year", 
    y = "NMFS Survey Biomass (1,000 t)",
    color = "Scenario",
    subtitle = "Points/Bars: Shared Observations",
    caption = "Error bars represent 95% log-normal confidence intervals on observations."
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~maturity, ncol = 1) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_idx_final)

```{r mmbfits, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Model fits to the observed mature biomass at survey (1,000 t), for all models presented."}

# --- 1. Process Prediction Data and Add Hybrid Status ---
dfrIndxFit_plot <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Index_fit_summary") |> 
  dplyr::filter(case != "25.1 gmacs" & maturity != "immature") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    across(c(year, obs, base_CV, actual_CV, q, prd, prsn_res), as.numeric)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::rename(
    predicted = prd,
    residuals = prsn_res,
    model     = case
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Categorize models based on the long label *before* shortening it
    hybrid_status = ifelse(grepl("hyb_surv|hyb_both", model, ignore.case = TRUE),
                           "Hybrid Included",
                           "Standard Survey"),
    maturity_status = ifelse(grepl("new_mat", model, ignore.case = TRUE),
                           "New maturity",
                           "Old maturity"),
    # Compact shortname for the legend
    model = to_short(model),
    # Confidence interval calculations
    sd_log = sqrt(log(1 + actual_CV^2)),
    lba    = qlnorm(0.05, log(obs), sd_log),
    uba    = qlnorm(0.95, log(obs), sd_log)
  )

check <- dfrIndxFit_plot %>%
  filter(year == 2019 & sex == "male") %>%
  select(sex, hybrid_status, maturity_status, obs, model)

# --- 2. Extract Unique Observations ---
# This ensures we only plot a single set of points and black error bars
dfrObs <- dfrIndxFit_plot |> 
  dplyr::distinct(year, sex, hybrid_status, maturity_status, obs, lba, uba)

# --- 3. Generate the 4-Panel Plot ---
p_idx_final <- ggplot() +
  # Model Predictions (Colored lines, plotted first so they sit behind points)
  geom_line(
    data = dfrIndxFit_plot, 
    aes(x = year, y = predicted, color = model), 
    lwd = 0.9, 
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  # Observations (Single black error bar per year/sex/panel)
  geom_errorbar(
    data = dfrObs,
    aes(x = year, ymin = lba, ymax = uba), 
    width = 0.3, 
    color = "black",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  # Observations (Single black point per year/sex/panel)
  geom_point(
    data = dfrObs,
    aes(x = year, y = obs), 
    size = 1.2,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  # Formatting and Scales
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    x = "Year", 
    y = "NMFS Survey Biomass (1,000 t)",
    color = "Model Prediction",
    subtitle = "Points/Bars: Shared Observations | Lines: Model Fits",
    caption = "Error bars represent 95% log-normal confidence intervals on observations."
  ) +
  facet_grid(sex ~ hybrid_status + maturity_status, scales = "free_y") + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_idx_final)

```

```{r catchfits, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.width=8, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Model fits to catch data (1,000 t), for all models presented."}

# --- 1. Process Catch Fit Data and Add Hybrid Status ---
dfrCatFit_plot <- wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst, "Catch_fit_summary") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Ensure numeric types
    across(c(year, obs, cv, effort, HM, prd, rsd), as.numeric)
  ) |> 
  dplyr::rename(
    predicted = prd,
    residuals = rsd,
    model     = case
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Identify if a model includes hybrid discards based on its long name
    hybrid_status = ifelse(grepl("hyb_both|hyb_fishery", model, ignore.case = TRUE),
                           "Hybrid Included",
                           "Standard Data"),
    # Compact shortname for the legend
    model = to_short(model),
    # Create descriptive row labels for faceting
    series = dplyr::case_when(
      fleet == "Trawl_Bycatch" ~ "Non-directed Bycatch",
      type == "retained" ~ "Directed Retained (Male)",
      type == "discard" & sex == "male"   ~ "Directed Discard (Male)",
      type == "discard" & sex == "female" ~ "Directed Discard (Female)",
      TRUE ~ paste(fleet, type, sex)
    )
  )

# --- 2. Extract Unique Observations ---
# This ensures that for models sharing the same data, only one point is plotted
dfrObs <- dfrCatFit_plot |> 
  dplyr::distinct(year, series, hybrid_status, obs)

# --- 3. Generate the 2-Column Comparison Plot ---
p_catch <- ggplot() +
  # 1. Model Predictions (Lines)
  geom_line(
    data = dfrCatFit_plot, 
    aes(x = year, y = predicted, color = model), 
    lwd = 0.8, 
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  # 2. Observations (Points)
  geom_point(
    data = dfrObs,
    aes(x = year, y = obs), 
    size = 1.2,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  # 3. Formatting and Scales
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    x = "Year", 
    y = "Catch (1,000 t)",
    color = "Model Scenario",
    title = "Fishery Catch and Bycatch Fits",
    subtitle = "Black points: Observations | Colored lines: Model predictions",
    caption = "Observations in the 'Hybrid Included' column contain hybrid crab discards (1,000 t). [[author: the hybrid cases are not in the September model set; drop this panel or label it as a May-cycle record.]]"
  ) +
  # Grid: Series (Rows) x Hybrid Status (Columns)
  facet_grid(series ~ hybrid_status, scales = "free_y") + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.title=element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text.y = element_text(size = 8, angle = 0), # Keep labels readable
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_catch)

```{r obs-101-vs-pred, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, out.width="100%", fig.width=6.5, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Estimated abundance of male crab >101mm carapace width from the survey (black line and dots with gray 95th CI) and from each model in the assessment (colored lines). [[author: the plotted quantity is the crabpack ABUNDANCE field divided by 1,000; state the resulting unit (thousands or millions of crab) -- it could not be established from the source.]]"}
EBSdata	<-read.csv("data/survey/survey_large_male_index_derived.csv")
EBSdata	<-EBSdata[EBSdata$CATEGORY=="preferred_male",]
#==make upper and lower CIs
EBSdata$upper_bio_ci<-exp(log(EBSdata$BIOMASS_MT)+1.96*(sqrt(log(1+EBSdata$BIOMASS_MT_CV^2))))
EBSdata$lower_bio_ci<-exp(log(EBSdata$BIOMASS_MT)-1.96*(sqrt(log(1+EBSdata$BIOMASS_MT_CV^2))))
EBSdata$upper_abn_ci<-exp(log(EBSdata$ABUNDANCE)+1.96*(sqrt(log(1+EBSdata$ABUNDANCE_CV^2))))
EBSdata$lower_abn_ci<-exp(log(EBSdata$ABUNDANCE)-1.96*(sqrt(log(1+EBSdata$ABUNDANCE_CV^2))))

#==take predicted survey
dfrN_YXMSZ = wtsGMACS::extractRep1Results(reslst,"N_YXMSZ") |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols=!c(case,year,sex,maturity,shell_con),
                      names_to="size",
                      values_to="est") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(year,size,est),
                              as.numeric),
                xm=paste(maturity,sex)
  );

  dplyr::summarize(ABN=3/5*sum(est))

pred_101_n2$tot_ABN<-(pred_101_n2$ABN+pred_101_n3$ABN)

# Shortnames for the color legend
pred_101_n2$case <- to_short(pred_101_n2$case)


male_101<-EBSdata
div_n<-1000
large_males2<-ggplot()+

  geom_point(data=male_101,aes(x=YEAR,y=ABUNDANCE/div_n))+

# Weight-at-size for mature males (kg per crab) from the report model.

  dplyr::filter(Sex == "male", Year == 1982, Maturity == "mature")
male_wt_lookup <- data.frame(

  dplyr::left_join(male_wt_lookup, by = "size") |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, case) |>
  dplyr::summarize(BIO = sum(est * wt), .groups = "drop")

pred_101_b3 <- filter(dfrN_YXMSZ, sex == 'male' & size == 97.5) |>
  dplyr::left_join(male_wt_lookup, by = "size") |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, case) |>
  dplyr::summarize(BIO = 3/5 * sum(est * wt), .groups = "drop")

pred_101_b2$tot_BIO <- pred_101_b2$BIO + pred_101_b3$BIO
pred_101_b2$case <- to_short(pred_101_b2$case)

```{r predfmort, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, fig.cap="Estimated fishing mortalities (per year) for the directed and non-directed fisheries."}

# --- 1. Robust Data Extraction across Models ---
# We loop through all models in reslst to find the correctly named F-dataframe
dfrF_plot <- names(reslst$repsLst) |> 
  purrr::map_dfr(function(c_name) {
    rep_obj <- reslst$repsLst[[c_name]]
    
    # Identify which name this specific model run used
    f_df_name <- intersect(
      names(rep_obj), 
      c("Fully-selected_capture_rate_by_season_sex_and_fishery", 
        "Fully-selected_FM_by_season_sex_and_fishery")
    )[1]
    
    if (is.na(f_df_name)) return(NULL)
    
    # Extract and clean
    rep_obj[[f_df_name]] |> 
      dplyr::mutate(
        Model = c_name,
        # Ensure consistency across versions (some use 'year', others 'Year')
        Year = as.numeric(year)
      )
  })

# --- 2. Clean and Filter Data for Plotting ---
plot_dat <- dfrF_plot |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Rename fleets for the report
    Fleet = dplyr::case_when(
      fleet == "Pot_Fishery" ~ "Directed Pot Fishery",
      fleet == "Trawl_Bycatch" ~ "Non-directed Bycatch",
      TRUE ~ fleet
    ),
    # Capitalize sex for headers
    Sex = stringr::str_to_title(sex),
    # Ensure mortality values are numeric (assuming season 2 is the primary fishery)
    F_value = as.numeric(`2`),
    # Compact shortname for the legend
    Model   = to_short(Model)
  ) |>
  # Filter only for the primary fishing fleets
  dplyr::filter(Fleet %in% c("Directed Pot Fishery", "Non-directed Bycatch"))

# --- 3. Generate the Comparison Plot ---
p_f_mort <- ggplot(plot_dat, aes(x = Year, y = F_value, color = Model, group = Model)) +
  # Model estimates
  geom_line(lwd = 1.1, alpha = 0.7) +
  # Layout and Scales
  facet_grid(Fleet ~ Sex, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated Fully-Selected Fishing Mortality",
    subtitle = "Calculated for the primary fishing season (Season 2)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Fishing Mortality (F)",
    color = element_blank()
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_f_mort)

```{r predmat, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=F, fig.height=8, fig.width=6.5, fig.cap="Estimated (black line) or specified (colored lines) probability(s) of maturing for male crab."}
# --- 1. Extract and Process Maturity Data ---
# case_for_data_table can be a single string or a vector of strings
plotdat_all <- case_for_mat_plot %>%
  purrr::map_dfr(function(case_name) {
    # Access the output list directly
    dat <- reslst$outsLst[[case_name]]$mature_probability
    
    if (is.null(dat)) {
      message("Warning: No mature_probability data for ", case_name)
      return(NULL)
    }
    
    # Pivot from wide to long format
    dat %>%
      tidyr::pivot_longer(
        cols = -c(Sex, Year),
        names_to = "width",
        values_to = "prob"
      ) %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        # Compact shortname for the legend
        Model = as.character(to_short(case_name)),
        # Logic to separate models with "newmat" (uses long label for the test)
        Maturity_Source = ifelse(grepl("new_mat", case_name, ignore.case = TRUE),
                                 "New Maturity Workflow",
                                 "Standard Maturity Data"),
        width = as.numeric(as.character(width)),
        prob = as.numeric(prob),
        # Ensure Year is a factor for discrete coloring if desired,
        # or keep numeric for a gradient
        Year_Fact = as.factor(Year)
      )
  })

# --- 2. Generate the Split Plot ---
p_molt <- plotdat_all %>%
  mutate(Year = as.numeric(Year)) %>%
 ggplot(aes(x = width, y = prob, color = Year_Fact)) +
  # Use group to ensure lines are drawn per Year/Model combination
  geom_line(lwd = 1.1, alpha = 0.7) +
  # Force y-axis from 0 to 1
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Carapace Width (mm)", 
    y = "Probability of Terminal Molt",
    col = "Year",
    title = "Probability of Maturing / Terminal Molt",
    subtitle = "Separated by Maturity Data Specification"
  ) +
  # Facet rows by Data Source (Standard vs Newmat) and columns by Sex
  facet_grid(Maturity_Source ~ Sex) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

# Render the plot
print(p_molt)

    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )

print(p_nat_m)

# Size composition fits

```{r size-comp-plots, results='asis', echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.width="100%"}

# Order comp plots by base fleet, comp_type, sex, maturity so that fits across
# model variants (hybrid/compfix/plus_group; new vs. old maturity ogive) for
# the same data block sit next to each other.
img_folder <- "plots"
img_files  <- list.files(path = img_folder, pattern = "^size_comp_plot_", full.names = TRUE)

parse_meta <- function(f) {
  base  <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  desc  <- sub("^size_comp_plot_\\d+_", "", base)
  parts <- strsplit(desc, "_")[[1]]
  sex_idx <- which(parts %in% c("male", "female"))[1]
  if (is.na(sex_idx)) {
    return(data.frame(file = f, fleet_full = NA_character_, base_fleet = NA_character_,
                      comp_type = NA_character_, sex = NA_character_,
                      maturity = NA_character_, ogive = NA_character_,
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
  }
  fleet_full <- paste(parts[seq_len(sex_idx - 1)], collapse = "_")
  sex        <- parts[sex_idx]
  comp_type  <- parts[sex_idx + 1]
  maturity   <- parts[sex_idx + 2]
  ogive      <- if (sex_idx + 3 <= length(parts))
                  paste(parts[seq(sex_idx + 3, length(parts))], collapse = "_") else NA_character_
  base_fleet <- tolower(fleet_full)
  base_fleet <- sub("_(hybrid|compfix|plus_group)$", "", base_fleet)
  data.frame(file = f, fleet_full = fleet_full, base_fleet = base_fleet,
             comp_type = comp_type, sex = sex, maturity = maturity, ogive = ogive,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

meta <- do.call(rbind, lapply(img_files, parse_meta))

meta$comp_type <- factor(meta$comp_type, levels = c("retained", "total", "discarded"))
meta$sex       <- factor(meta$sex,       levels = c("female", "male"))
meta$maturity  <- factor(meta$maturity,  levels = c("immature", "mature", "undetermined"))

meta <- meta[order(meta$base_fleet, meta$comp_type, meta$sex, meta$maturity,
                   meta$fleet_full, meta$ogive), ]

make_caption <- function(f) {
  base <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  desc <- sub("^size_comp_plot_\\d+_", "", base)
  desc <- gsub("_", " ", desc)
  paste0("Model fits (lines) to size composition data (grey bars): ", desc, ".")
}

# Initialize trackers with empty strings
last_fleet <- ""
last_sex_mat <- ""

for (i in 1:nrow(meta)) {
  row <- meta[i, ]
  
  # 1. Check for Fleet change (## Header)
  if (row$base_fleet != last_fleet) {
    # Print the header (cleaning up underscores for readability)
    cat("\n## Fleet: ", tools::toTitleCase(gsub("_", " ", row$base_fleet)), "\n\n")
    
    # Update tracker
    last_fleet <- row$base_fleet
    # Reset sex_mat tracker so it prints for the new fleet section 
    # even if it's the same category as the end of the last fleet
    last_sex_mat <- "" 
  }
  
  # 2. Check for Sex/Maturity change (### Header)
  current_sex_mat <- paste(row$sex, "and", row$maturity)
  if (current_sex_mat != last_sex_mat) {
    cat("\n### ", tools::toTitleCase(current_sex_mat), "\n\n")
    last_sex_mat <- current_sex_mat
  }
  
  # 3. Print the Plot
  cat("![", make_caption(row$file), "](", URLencode(row$file), ")\n\n", sep = "")
  
  # Optional: Add page break after every plot, or move this inside the header 
  # logic if you only want page breaks between fleets.
  cat("\\newpage\n\n")
}


```
